lessons.title: Key Facts
lessons.notes_html:
Facts to Remember

  • Mendeleev in his periodic table, arranged the elements according to their atomic masses.
  • Vertical columns in the modern periodic table are called groups and horizontal rows are called periods.
  • Members of group VIIA are called halogens and alkali metals is the family name of group IA members.
  • Metals form basic oxides and non-metals form acidic oxides.
  • Hydrogen can be placed above the groups IA, IVA and VIIA of the periodic table.
  • Shielding effect is actually the repulsion due to electrons in between the nucleus and the outermost shell.
  • Noble gases have the highest values of ionization energy due to their complete outermost shells.
  • When a second electron is added to a uni-negative ion, the incoming electron is repelled by the already present negative charge.
  • Due to having partly filled d-orbitals, transition metals usually show variable valency.
  • Melting and boiling points of halogens increase down the group.
  • In Mendeleev's periodic table elements Be, Mg, Zn and Cd are placed in the same group. — True.
  • The second and third periods contain eighteen elements each. — False.
  • Alkaline earth metals are present in Group IIA. — True.
  • Metals are present in the top right corner of the periodic table. — False.
  • Metalloids are present in the lower half of Groups IVA, VA and VIA. — True.
  • Hydrogen forms uni-negative ion like halogens. — True.
  • Oxidation state of an element is related to the number of period it belongs. — False.
  • Diamond is a good conductor of electricity. — False.
  • Melting points of halogens decrease down the group. — False.
  • Zinc oxide is an example of amphoteric oxide. — True.

Periodic Trends

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Q4. What are the improvements made in Mendeleev's periodic table?
Mendeleev's table was improved when elements were arranged by atomic number instead of atomic mass. This removed the wrong order of some pairs, like argon and potassium, and tellurium and iodine. The modern table also gives separate places to isotopes and to the noble gases. It explains periodicity clearly through electronic configuration and group numbers.

Q5. How does classification of elements in different blocks help in understanding their chemistry?
Block classification groups elements by the subshell being filled: s, p, d or f. Elements of one block have similar outer electronic configurations, so their chemistry is similar. It predicts valency, oxidation states and whether an element is a metal or non-metal. Thus the whole chemistry of an element can be roughly predicted from its block and position.

Q6. How do you justify the position of hydrogen at the top of various groups?
Hydrogen resembles group IA metals: it has one outer electron and forms a positive ion. It resembles halogens: it needs one electron for a stable shell and forms a negative ion. It resembles group IVA elements: its valence shell is half-filled and it forms covalent bonds. Because it matches no group fully, it is placed at the top, usually above group IA.

Q7. Why are the ionic radii of negative ions larger than the size of their parent atoms?
A negative ion is formed when an atom gains one or more electrons. The number of protons stays the same, but the electrons now repel each other more strongly. The electron cloud therefore expands and the effective nuclear pull on each electron falls. So the anion is always larger than its parent neutral atom.

Q8. Why does ionization energy decrease down the group and increase along a period?
Down a group, new shells are added, so the outer electron is farther from the nucleus. Inner electrons also shield the outer electron, so less energy is needed to remove it. Along a period, electrons enter the same shell while the nuclear charge increases. The stronger pull holds electrons tighter, so ionization energy increases along a period.

Q9. Why is the second value of electron affinity of an element usually shown with a positive sign?
The first electron affinity is exothermic because the neutral atom attracts the electron. Adding a second electron means forcing it into an already negative ion. The incoming electron is repelled, so energy must be supplied from outside. Energy absorbed is shown with a positive sign, so the second electron affinity is positive.

Q10. Why does metallic character increase from top to bottom in a group of metals?
Metallic character depends on how easily an atom loses its outer electrons. Down a group, atomic size increases and shielding by inner shells also increases. The outer electrons are held less tightly by the nucleus. They are lost more easily, so metallic character increases down the group.

mcqs.why: The notes state that down a group new shells are added, the outer electron is farther away and shielded, so less energy is needed to remove it.

mcqs.why: The notes state that along a period electrons enter the same shell while nuclear charge increases, so the stronger pull makes ionization energy increase.

The second electron enters a new shell and is shielded

lessons.title: Long Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Q11. Explain the variation in melting points along the short periods.
Along a short period, melting and boiling points first increase from left to right up to the middle of the period and then decrease. The increase is due to stronger metallic bonding as the number of delocalised electrons and nuclear charge increase. After the middle, elements form discrete covalent molecules (for example P4, S8, Cl2) held by weak van der Waals forces, so melting points fall, and noble gases have the lowest values.

Q12. Why is the oxidation state of noble gases usually zero?
Noble gases have completely filled outermost shells (ns2np6, except helium 1s2), which is a very stable configuration. They have very high ionization energies and positive electron affinities, so they neither lose nor gain electrons readily. Their oxidation state is therefore usually zero, and they remain chemically inert under ordinary conditions.

Q13. Why is diamond a non-conductor and graphite fairly a good conductor?
In diamond, every carbon atom is sp3 hybridised and bonded to four others in a rigid three-dimensional network. All valence electrons are used in covalent bonds, so there are no free or mobile electrons to carry current, and diamond is a non-conductor. In graphite, each carbon is sp2 hybridised and bonded to three others in layers, with one delocalised pi electron per carbon free to move between layers, so graphite conducts electricity fairly well.

Q14. Give brief reasons for (a)-(h) as listed in the book.
(a) d- and f-block elements are called transition elements because their d or f subshells are partially filled in the atom or in a common oxidation state, giving them transitional properties between s- and p-blocks. (b) Lanthanide contraction is the steady decrease in atomic size across the lanthanides, caused by poor shielding by f electrons; it makes the 6th-period transition metals almost the same size as the 5th-period ones above them. (c) Melting and boiling points rise up to the middle of the s- and p-blocks because metallic bonding strengthens with more delocalised electrons, then fall because the elements become molecular or gaseous with weak intermolecular forces. (d) Oxidation states vary in a period because the number of valence electrons changes across the period, while in a group the valence electron count stays the same, so the common oxidation states remain almost constant. (e) Hydration energy depends on charge density: Al3+ is small and highly charged, Mg2+ is intermediate, and Na+ is larger and singly charged, so hydration energy follows Al3+ > Mg2+ > Na+. (f) Ionic character of halides decreases from left to right in a period because the metal becomes less electropositive and the bond becomes more covalent (Fajans' rules). (g) Alkali metals are strongly electropositive and their hydrides are ionic: the metal loses its outer electron completely to hydrogen, giving M+ H-. (h) Sodium and phosphorus are in the same period, but sodium is a metal and forms the basic oxide Na2O, while phosphorus is a non-metal and forms the acidic oxide P2O5, because metallic character decreases across a period.

mcqs.q: How do melting and boiling points vary along a short period?
options: They decrease continuously from left to right
They increase continuously from left to right
They first increase from left to right up to the middle of the period and then decrease
They remain constant across the period
mcqs.why: The notes state that along a short period melting and boiling points first increase up to the middle of the period and then decrease.

mcqs.q: Why do melting points increase up to the middle of a short period?
options: The elements form discrete covalent molecules with weak forces
The elements become noble gases with low values
Van der Waals forces become weaker
Metallic bonding becomes stronger as the number of delocalised electrons and nuclear charge increase
mcqs.why: The notes attribute the increase to stronger metallic bonding as the number of delocalised electrons and nuclear charge increase.

mcqs.q: Why do melting points fall after the middle of a short period?
options: Elements form discrete covalent molecules such as P4, S8 and Cl2 held by weak van der Waals forces
Metallic bonding becomes strongest at the end of the period
The number of delocalised electrons keeps increasing
Noble gases have the highest melting points
mcqs.why: The notes state that after the middle, elements form discrete covalent molecules (P4, S8, Cl2) held by weak van der Waals forces, so melting points fall.

mcqs.q: Why is the oxidation state of noble gases usually zero?
options: They have completely filled outermost shells (ns2np6, except helium 1s2), a very stable configuration
They have low ionization energies and negative electron affinities
They readily lose and gain electrons
mcqs.why: The notes state noble gases have completely filled outermost shells, very high ionization energies and positive electron affinities, so their oxidation state is usually zero.

mcqs.q: Why is diamond a non-conductor of electricity?
options: Each carbon has one delocalised pi electron free to move between layers
Carbon atoms in diamond are arranged in flat layers
Every carbon is sp3 hybridised and bonded to four others, so all valence electrons are used in bonds and none are free to carry current
Diamond contains mobile ions that cancel the current
mcqs.why: The notes state that in diamond all valence electrons are used in covalent bonds in a rigid three-dimensional network, so there are no free electrons to carry current.

mcqs.q: In graphite, to how many other carbon atoms is each carbon atom bonded?
mcqs.why: Working: the notes say each graphite carbon is sp2 hybridised and bonded to three others, with one delocalised pi electron per carbon; 3 bonds to other carbons + 1 delocalised pi electron = 4 valence connections, so the answer is 3 (verified: 4 - 1 = 3).

mcqs.q: What causes the lanthanide contraction?
options: Poor shielding by f electrons, causing a steady decrease in atomic size across the lanthanides
Strong shielding by f electrons, causing a steady increase in size
Partly filled d-orbitals in the lanthanides
The addition of new shells across the lanthanides
mcqs.why: The notes define lanthanide contraction as the steady decrease in atomic size across the lanthanides caused by poor shielding by f electrons.

mcqs.q: What is the order of hydration energy for Al3+, Mg2+ and Na+ given in the notes?
mcqs.why: Working: hydration energy depends on charge density; charges are Al = 3+, Mg = 2+, Na = 1+, and Al3+ is small while Na+ is larger, so the order by charge is 3 > 2 > 1, giving Al3+ > Mg2+ > Na+ as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: Why are the hydrides of alkali metals ionic in nature?
options: The metal shares its outer electron equally with hydrogen
Hydrogen loses its electron to the metal, giving M- H+
The metal loses its outer electron completely to hydrogen, giving M+ H-
The hydrides contain partly filled d-orbitals
mcqs.why: The notes state that alkali metals are strongly electropositive and their hydrides are ionic because the metal loses its outer electron completely to hydrogen, giving M+ H-.

mcqs.q: Sodium and phosphorus are in the same period, but their oxides differ how?
options: Sodium forms the acidic oxide Na2O, while phosphorus forms the basic oxide P2O5
Both form the basic oxide Na2O
Both form the acidic oxide P2O5
Sodium forms the basic oxide Na2O, while phosphorus forms the acidic oxide P2O5
mcqs.why: The notes state sodium is a metal forming basic Na2O and phosphorus is a non-metal forming acidic P2O5, because metallic character decreases across a period.

lessons.title: Key Facts
lessons.notes_html:
Facts to Remember

  • Alkali metals are more reactive than alkaline-earth metals.
  • Alkali metals decompose water vigorously producing alkalies and hydrogen.
  • When heated in a current of dry hydrogen, alkaline earth metals form white crystalline hydrides of the type MH2.
  • The beryllium hydroxide, like the hydroxide of aluminium, is amphoteric, while the hydroxides of the other members of group IIA are basic.
  • The elements of group IA are termed as alkali metals, because their hydroxides are alkaline.
  • Spodumene is an ore of lithium metal.
  • Alkali metal nitrates on heating give the corresponding nitrites and oxygen.
  • Na2CO3.H2O is the chemical formula of a mineral of sodium which is known as natron.
  • Metallic bicarbonates are decomposed on heating into their carbonates, along with water and carbon dioxide.
  • Metal nitrates other than the alkali metals on heating decompose into the corresponding metal oxides along with nitrogen peroxide and oxygen.
  • Group IA elements are called alkali metals because their chlorides are alkaline in nature. — False.
  • Alkali metals are very good conductors of electricity. — True.
  • The hydroxides of alkali metals and alkaline-earth metals are soluble in water. — False.
  • Plaster of Paris is a hemihydrate. — True.
  • Alkali metals have low melting and boiling points as compared to those of alkaline earth metals. — True.
  • Lithium carbonate is decomposed to its oxide, but the carbonates of the other alkali metals are stable towards heat. — True.
  • All alkali metal sulphates are insoluble in water. — False.
  • Lithium combines with nitrogen to form lithium nitride but other alkali metals do not react with nitrogen. — True.
  • Trona is a mineral of lithium. — False.
  • Alkaline earth metals are stronger reducing agents than alkali metals. — False.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Q4(a). Give the names, electronic configurations and occurrence of s-block elements.
Group IA (alkali metals): Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr, with outer configuration ns1. Group IIA (alkaline-earth metals): Be, Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba, Ra, with outer configuration ns2. They are very reactive, so they never occur free in nature. They occur as chlorides, carbonates, sulphates and silicates in rocks, sea water and minerals.

Q4(b). Discuss the peculiar behaviour of lithium with respect to the other members of alkali metals.
Lithium is very small in size with high charge density, so it behaves differently. Its salts are less soluble, its carbonate and nitrate decompose on heating, unlike other alkali metals. It forms a nitride with nitrogen directly, while other alkali metals do not. It resembles magnesium diagonally, which is called diagonal relationship.

Q5. Discuss the trends in chemical properties of compounds like oxides, hydroxides, carbonates, nitrates and sulphates of IA and IIA group elements.
Oxides and hydroxides of both groups are basic, and their basic strength increases down the group. Carbonates of alkali metals are stable to heat, but alkaline-earth carbonates decompose on heating. Alkali metal nitrates give nitrites on heating, while other nitrates give oxides, NO2 and oxygen. Sulphates of alkali metals are soluble, but sulphates of heavier alkaline-earth metals are insoluble.

Q7(b). Why is the aqueous solution of Na2CO3 alkaline in nature?
Sodium carbonate is a salt of a strong base, NaOH, and a weak acid, carbonic acid. In water it hydrolyses to give sodium hydroxide and carbonic acid. The free hydroxide ions make the solution alkaline. That is why washing soda solution feels soapy and turns red litmus blue.

Q8(a). Describe with a diagram the manufacture of sodium by Down's cell.
In Down's cell, fused sodium chloride mixed with calcium chloride is electrolysed. The mixture melts near 600 C, much lower than pure NaCl, which saves fuel. At the iron cathode, sodium ions gain electrons and molten sodium collects. At the graphite anode, chloride ions lose electrons and chlorine gas is released.

Q8(b). Point out the three advantages of this process.
First, the low melting mixture saves heat energy and cost. Second, sodium and chlorine are obtained at the same time, both useful products. Third, the cell runs continuously, so sodium is produced on a large scale.

Q11(a). Why are alkali and alkaline earth metals among the reactive elements of the periodic table?
They have only one or two electrons in their outermost shell. These electrons are far from the nucleus and are shielded by inner shells. Very little energy is needed to remove them, so the metals react readily. They act as strong reducing agents in almost all their reactions.

Q11(c). How is gypsum converted into plaster of Paris?
Gypsum is calcium sulphate dihydrate, CaSO4.2H2O. When it is heated to about 120 C, it loses three quarters of its water of crystallisation. The product is calcium sulphate hemihydrate, CaSO4.1/2H2O. This hemihydrate is plaster of Paris, which sets hard again when mixed with water.

Q11(e). Why is lime added to an acidic soil?
Acidic soil contains excess hydrogen ions which harm plant roots. Lime, calcium oxide or calcium hydroxide, neutralises this acidity. It supplies calcium, an important plant nutrient, to the soil. It also improves soil structure, so air and water move better through it.

mcqs.why: The notes state lithium resembles magnesium diagonally, which is called diagonal relationship.

options: Both groups' carbonates decompose readily on heating
Alkaline-earth carbonates are stable, but alkali carbonates decompose
Neither group's carbonates is affected by heat

mcqs.why: The notes state carbonates of alkali metals are stable to heat, but alkaline-earth carbonates decompose on heating; lithium carbonate is the alkali exception noted elsewhere in the notes.

mcqs.q: Why is the aqueous solution of Na2CO3 alkaline in nature?
options: It is a salt of a strong base, NaOH, and a weak acid, carbonic acid, and hydrolyses to give free hydroxide ions
It is a salt of a weak base and a strong acid
It dissolves to give free hydrogen ions
It reacts with water to give carbonic acid only
mcqs.why: The notes state sodium carbonate hydrolyses to give sodium hydroxide and carbonic acid, and the free hydroxide ions make the solution alkaline, turning red litmus blue.

mcqs.q: In Down's cell, the fused sodium chloride is mixed with calcium chloride so that the mixture melts near which temperature?
mcqs.why: The notes state that in Down's cell the fused NaCl mixed with CaCl2 melts near 600 C, much lower than pure NaCl, which saves fuel.

mcqs.q: In Down's cell, what is produced at the iron cathode?
options: Chlorine gas, as chloride ions lose electrons
Hydrogen gas, as water is reduced
Molten sodium, as sodium ions gain electrons
Calcium metal, as calcium ions gain electrons
mcqs.why: The notes state that at the iron cathode sodium ions gain electrons and molten sodium collects, while chlorine gas is released at the graphite anode.

mcqs.q: Gypsum, CaSO4.2H2O, is heated to about 120 C to make plaster of Paris. How much water of crystallisation remains per formula unit?
mcqs.why: Working: water present = 2; fraction lost = 3/4; water lost = 2 x 3/4 = 1.5; water remaining = 2 - 1.5 = 0.5. The product is therefore CaSO4.1/2H2O, the hemihydrate plaster of Paris (verified: 2 x (1 - 3/4) = 0.5).

lessons.title: Long Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Q6. Compare the chemical behaviour of lithium with magnesium.
Lithium resembles magnesium (diagonal relationship) because both are small with high charge density. Both form normal oxides (not peroxides or superoxides) and nitrides by direct combination with nitrogen, while other alkali metals do not. Their carbonates, hydroxides and nitrates decompose on heating (lithium carbonate to oxide, magnesium carbonate to oxide), and their chlorides are covalent and soluble in organic solvents.

Q7(a). Mention the properties of beryllium in which it does not resemble its own family.
Beryllium does not resemble its own family in several ways: it is very small with high charge density, so its compounds are largely covalent rather than ionic. Its oxide and hydroxide are amphoteric, while other group IIA oxides and hydroxides are basic. It does not react with water, does not form a stable carbonate, and forms complexes, resembling aluminium (diagonal relationship) rather than magnesium.

Q9(a). Compare the physical and chemical properties of alkali metals with those of alkaline earth metals.
Physical properties: alkali metals are softer, lighter, and have lower melting and boiling points than alkaline earth metals, because they have only one outer electron and weaker metallic bonding. Both are good conductors of electricity and heat, but alkaline earth metals are harder and denser. Chemical properties: both are very reactive and strong reducing agents, but alkali metals are more reactive; alkali metals form M+ ions and normal oxides, while alkaline earth metals form M2+ ions and are less vigorous with water.

Q9(b). What happens when: (i) lithium carbonate is heated, (ii) lithium hydroxide is heated to red hot, (iii) beryllium is treated with sodium hydroxide, (iv) lithium hydride is treated with water?
(i) Lithium carbonate on heating gives lithium oxide and carbon dioxide: Li2CO3 gives Li2O + CO2. (ii) Lithium hydroxide heated to red heat gives lithium oxide and water: 2 LiOH gives Li2O + H2O. (iii) Beryllium with sodium hydroxide gives sodium beryllate and hydrogen: Be + 2 NaOH gives Na2BeO2 + H2. (iv) Lithium hydride with water gives lithium hydroxide and hydrogen: LiH + H2O gives LiOH + H2.

Q10. Give formulas of: (a) dolomite, (b) asbestos, (c) halite, (d) natron, (e) beryl, (f) sylvite, (g) phosphorite, (h) Chile saltpetre.
(a) Dolomite is CaMg(CO3)2 (CaCO3.MgCO3). (b) Asbestos is CaMg3(SiO3)4. (c) Halite is NaCl. (d) Natron is Na2CO3.H2O. (e) Beryl is Be3Al2(SiO3)6. (f) Sylvite is KCl. (g) Phosphorite is Ca3(PO4)2. (h) Chile saltpetre is NaNO3.

Q11(b,d,f,g). Answer briefly: (b) lime water with CO2, (d) 2% gypsum in cement, (f) lime and sand for glass, (g) lime mortar.
(b) Lime water turns milky with carbon dioxide because insoluble calcium carbonate is formed: Ca(OH)2 + CO2 gives CaCO3 + H2O. With excess carbon dioxide it becomes clear because the carbonate converts to soluble calcium hydrogen carbonate: CaCO3 + CO2 + H2O gives Ca(HCO3)2. (d) 2% gypsum is added to cement to control its setting: it reacts with tricalcium aluminate and prevents flash setting, so the cement sets at a workable rate. (f) Lime and sand are used to make glass: limestone (CaO), sand (SiO2) and soda ash are melted together to give soda-lime glass, a calcium sodium silicate. (g) Lime mortar is prepared by mixing slaked lime, Ca(OH)2, with sand and water; it hardens by absorbing carbon dioxide from air to form calcium carbonate, which binds the sand.

lessons.notes_html:
Q4. What is the action of an aqueous solution of borax on litmus?
An aqueous solution of borax is alkaline in nature. On hydrolysis it gives sodium hydroxide and boric acid. The free alkali turns red litmus paper blue. Blue litmus paper remains unchanged in borax solution.

Q5(a). Give the equation: borax is heated with CoO.
Borax first loses water and swells up, then melts to a clear glassy bead. The bead is sodium metaborate and boric anhydride. Cobalt oxide dissolves in the bead and forms cobalt metaborate. CoO + B2O3 gives Co(BO2)2, which colours the bead deep blue.

Q6. Why is aluminium not found as a free element? Explain the chemistry of the borax bead test.
Aluminium is very reactive and has a strong attraction for oxygen. In nature it is always found combined, mainly as oxides and silicates. In the borax bead test, borax is heated on a platinum loop until it forms a glassy bead. A coloured metal oxide dissolved in the bead gives a characteristic colour, which identifies the metal.

Q7. How does orthoboric acid react with: (a) sodium hydroxide (b) ethyl alcohol?
(a) With sodium hydroxide, orthoboric acid gives sodium borate and water. H3BO3 + NaOH gives NaBO2 + 2H2O, and with excess alkali it gives borax. (b) With ethyl alcohol in the presence of concentrated sulphuric acid it forms triethyl borate. Triethyl borate burns with a green-edged flame, which is a test for boric acid.

Q9. Why are liquid silicones preferred over ordinary organic lubricants?
Liquid silicones keep their viscosity over a very wide range of temperature. They do not freeze easily in cold and do not thin out much in heat. They are chemically inert and are not attacked by water or oxidising agents. They are also good electrical insulators, so they serve in machines and electrical parts.

Q10(a). CO2 is non-polar in nature. (b) CO2 is acidic in character.
(a) Carbon dioxide is linear, O=C=O, so the two C=O dipoles are equal and opposite. They cancel each other, so the molecule has no net dipole moment and is non-polar. (b) When CO2 dissolves in water it forms carbonic acid, H2CO3. It turns blue litmus red and reacts with alkalies to form carbonates, showing acidic character.

Q11. Why is CO2 a gas at room temperature while SiO2 is a solid?
Carbon dioxide exists as small separate molecules held by weak van der Waals forces. Very little energy is needed to separate them, so CO2 is a gas. Silicon dioxide forms a giant covalent network in which every silicon is bonded to oxygen atoms. Breaking this strong network needs great energy, so SiO2 is a hard solid with a high melting point.

mcqs.why: The notes state CO2 exists as small separate molecules held by weak van der Waals forces, while SiO2 forms a giant covalent network, so it is a hard solid with a high melting point.

lessons.title: Long Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Q5(b). Give the equation: Al2O3 is heated with NaOH solution.
Aluminium oxide heated with sodium hydroxide solution gives sodium aluminate and water: Al2O3 + 2 NaOH gives 2 NaAlO2 + H2O. The reaction shows the amphoteric character of aluminium oxide, which reacts with both acids and bases. In solution the product is often written as sodium tetrahydroxoaluminate, Na[Al(OH)4].

Q8. How will you convert boric acid into borax and vice versa?
Boric acid is converted to borax by reacting it with sodium carbonate: 4 H3BO3 + Na2CO3 gives Na2B4O7 + CO2 + 6 H2O. Borax is converted back to boric acid by acidifying a hot concentrated solution of borax with sulphuric acid, on cooling boric acid crystallises out: Na2B4O7 + H2SO4 + 5 H2O gives Na2SO4 + 4 H3BO3.

Q12. Give the names and the formulas of different acids of boron.
The acids of boron are: orthoboric acid, H3BO3; metaboric acid, HBO2; pyroboric acid (tetraboric acid), H2B4O7; and boric anhydride (boron sesquioxide), B2O3, which gives these acids with water. Orthoboric acid is the common, stable acid, obtained from borax and from colemanite. Metaboric acid is formed when orthoboric acid is heated to about 100 C, and pyroboric acid on stronger heating.

Q13. What is the importance of oxides of lead in paints?
Oxides of lead are important in paints as pigments and driers: white lead, 2PbCO3.Pb(OH)2, is a white pigment with good covering power. Red lead, Pb3O4, is used as an anticorrosive primer for iron and steel, because it protects the metal from rusting. Litharge, PbO, is used in paints, in glass, and as a drier that speeds the drying of oil paints.

Q14. Give the names, electronic configurations and occurrence of Group IIIA elements.
Group IIIA elements are boron (B), aluminium (Al), gallium (Ga), indium (In) and thallium (Tl), with outer configuration ns2np1. Boron occurs as borax and colemanite; aluminium is the most abundant metal in the earth's crust, occurring as bauxite, cryolite and feldspar. Gallium, indium and thallium are rarer, occurring as traces in ores of zinc, aluminium and lead sulphides.

Q15. Discuss the peculiar behaviour of boron with respect to the other members of Group IIIA.
Boron behaves peculiarly compared with other group IIIA elements because it is very small and has no d orbitals, so its chemistry is covalent, not ionic. It is a non-metal and a semiconductor, while aluminium and the heavier members are metals. Boron forms electron-deficient compounds (for example BF3, which accepts an electron pair) and does not form a stable B3+ ion, unlike the others which show the +3 oxidation state.

Q16. (a) What is borax? (b) Its commercial preparation. (c) Principal uses. (d) How does borax serve as a water softening agent?
Borax is sodium tetraborate decahydrate, Na2B4O7.10H2O, a white crystalline solid. It is prepared commercially from colemanite (calcium borate) by boiling with sodium carbonate, which precipitates calcium carbonate and leaves sodium borate in solution, crystallised as borax; it also occurs naturally as tincal. Its uses are in glass, glazes, detergents, antiseptics, and the borax bead test. As a water softener, borax precipitates calcium and magnesium ions as insoluble borates, so soap is not wasted on hardness.

Q17. (a) What is boric acid? (b) Laboratory preparation. (c) Properties and uses.
Boric acid (orthoboric acid, H3BO3) is a weak, white crystalline acid. In the laboratory it is prepared by acidifying a hot concentrated solution of borax with dilute sulphuric acid and cooling, when boric acid crystallises out. Its properties are: it is a weak monobasic acid (it accepts OH- rather than donating H+ directly), it is soluble in hot water, and it gives a green flame with alcohol. Its uses are as an antiseptic (boric lotion for eyes), in glass, glazes, and as a food preservative in small amounts.

Q18. (a) Three important ores of aluminium. (b) How aluminium reacts with oxygen, hydrogen, halogens, acids and alkalies.
(a) Three important ores of aluminium are bauxite (Al2O3.2H2O), cryolite (Na3AlF6) and feldspar (KAlSi3O8). (b) Aluminium reacts: (i) with oxygen on heating to give aluminium oxide, 4 Al + 3 O2 gives 2 Al2O3; (ii) with hydrogen it does not react directly under ordinary conditions. (iii) With halogens it gives aluminium halides, for example 2 Al + 3 Cl2 gives 2 AlCl3. (iv) With acids it gives a salt and hydrogen, for example 2 Al + 6 HCl gives 2 AlCl3 + 3 H2. (v) With alkalies it gives an aluminate and hydrogen, for example 2 Al + 2 NaOH + 2 H2O gives 2 NaAlO2 + 3 H2.

Q19. Give the names, electronic configurations and occurrence of Group IVA elements.
Group IVA elements are carbon (C), silicon (Si), germanium (Ge), tin (Sn) and lead (Pb), with outer configuration ns2np2. Carbon occurs free as diamond and graphite and combined in carbonates, coal and petroleum; silicon is the second most abundant element in the crust, in silica and silicates. Germanium occurs in traces in zinc ores, tin as cassiterite (SnO2), and lead as galena (PbS).

Q20. Discuss the peculiar behaviour of carbon with respect to the other members of Group IVA.
Carbon behaves peculiarly compared with other group IVA elements because it is very small, has no d orbitals, and shows the strongest catenation (forming long chains and rings). It forms multiple bonds (C=C, C triple C) readily, while the heavier members rarely do, and it is the only member that is a non-metal in all its common forms. Carbon shows the +4 and -4 states and forms stable covalent compounds, while tin and lead show the +2 state prominently due to the inert pair effect.

Q21. (a) What are silicones? (b) Properties. (c) Uses. (d) What are silicates? (e) Uses of silicates.
(a) Silicones are organosilicon polymers with alternating silicon and oxygen atoms in the chain, with organic groups (usually methyl) attached to silicon. (b) Their principal properties are: they are stable over a wide temperature range, water-repellent, chemically inert, and keep their viscosity in heat and cold. (c) Their uses are as lubricants, water-repellent coatings, sealants, antifoams, and in cosmetics and medical implants. (d) Silicates are salts of silicic acids, built from SiO4 tetrahedra joined in chains, sheets or frameworks, and are the main minerals of rocks and clays. (e) Silicates are used in glass, cement, ceramics, zeolites (water softening and catalysis), and as fillers and building materials.

mcqs.why: The notes give group IIIA elements boron, aluminium, gallium, indium and thallium with outer configuration ns2np1.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Q4(i). How does nitrogen differ from other elements of its group?
Nitrogen is a gas, while phosphorus, arsenic, antimony and bismuth are solids. Its small size lets it form strong triple bonds, so N2 is very unreactive. It cannot expand its octet because it has no d-orbitals, so its maximum covalency is four. It forms no stable pentahalides, unlike phosphorus which forms PCl5.

Q4(ii). Why does aqua regia dissolve gold and platinum?
Aqua regia is a mixture of one part concentrated nitric acid and three parts concentrated hydrochloric acid. Nitric acid oxidises gold to gold ions, while hydrochloric acid supplies chloride ions. Gold ions combine with chloride to form the stable complex HAuCl4. The complex formation drives the reaction forward, so even noble metals dissolve.

Q4(iii). Why do the elements of group VIA other than oxygen show more than two oxidation states?
Oxygen has no d-orbitals, so it shows mainly -2, -1 and +2 oxidation states. Sulphur, selenium and tellurium have vacant d-orbitals in their valence shells. Their paired s and p electrons can be promoted to d-orbitals for bonding. They therefore show -2, +2, +4 and +6 oxidation states.

Q4(v). Write the equation for the reaction between conc. H2SO4 and copper, and explain what type of reaction it is.
Cu + 2H2SO4 gives CuSO4 + SO2 + 2H2O. Copper is oxidised from 0 to +2, while sulphur in the acid is reduced from +6 to +4. It is therefore an oxidation-reduction reaction. Concentrated sulphuric acid here acts as an oxidising agent, not simply as an acid.

lessons.title: Long Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Q4(iv). Write down a comparison of the properties of oxygen and sulphur.
Oxygen and sulphur differ in several ways: oxygen is a gas and sulphur is a solid at room temperature. Oxygen shows mainly the -2 oxidation state (and -1 in peroxides), while sulphur shows -2, +2, +4 and +6, because it can use d orbitals. Oxygen forms diatomic molecules (O2) with a double bond, while sulphur forms puckered S8 rings; oxygen is more electronegative and does not show catenation like sulphur.

Q5. (a) Birkeland and Eyde's process for nitric acid. (b) Which metals evolve hydrogen with nitric acid? (c) What is fuming nitric acid?
Birkeland and Eyde's process makes nitric acid from air: nitrogen and oxygen are heated to very high temperature (about 3000 C) in an electric arc, forming nitric oxide, N2 + O2 gives 2 NO. The nitric oxide is cooled and oxidised by air to nitrogen dioxide, 2 NO + O2 gives 2 NO2, which is absorbed in water to give nitric acid and nitric oxide, 3 NO2 + H2O gives 2 HNO3 + NO. (b) Most metals do not evolve hydrogen with nitric acid, because nitric acid is an oxidising acid; magnesium and manganese are exceptions and evolve hydrogen with very dilute nitric acid: Mg + 2 HNO3 (dilute) gives Mg(NO3)2 + H2. (c) Fuming nitric acid is concentrated nitric acid containing dissolved nitrogen dioxide, which gives it a reddish-brown colour and fumes in air.

Q6. (a) Sulphuric acid as acid, oxidising agent and dehydrating agent (two reactions each). (b) Advantages of the contact process.
As an acid, sulphuric acid reacts with bases to give salts and water, and with carbonates to give a salt, water and carbon dioxide. As an oxidising agent, it oxidises copper to copper sulphate with sulphur dioxide, and carbon to carbon dioxide with sulphur dioxide. As a dehydrating agent, it removes water from sugar (charring it black) and from formic acid (giving carbon monoxide), and it absorbs water from gases. Advantages of the contact process are: it gives a very pure, concentrated acid; sulphur dioxide is fully converted using a cheap catalyst (V2O5); and the process is continuous and economical on a large scale.

Q7. (a) Contact process from sulphur. (b) Why SO3 is dissolved in H2SO4 and not water. (c) Action of sulphuric acid on metals.
In the contact process, sulphur is burnt in air to sulphur dioxide: S + O2 gives SO2. Sulphur dioxide is oxidised to sulphur trioxide over vanadium pentoxide catalyst at about 450 C: 2 SO2 + O2 gives 2 SO3. Sulphur trioxide is absorbed in concentrated sulphuric acid to give oleum, SO3 + H2SO4 gives H2S2O7, which is diluted with water to sulphuric acid of the required strength. (b) SO3 is dissolved in H2SO4 and not in water because direct absorption in water is highly exothermic and forms a mist of acid that is difficult to condense; absorption in acid is smooth and controllable. (c) With metals, dilute sulphuric acid gives a salt and hydrogen (for example Zn + H2SO4 gives ZnSO4 + H2), while concentrated hot sulphuric acid acts as an oxidising agent (for example Cu + 2 H2SO4 gives CuSO4 + SO2 + 2 H2O).

Q8. Describe the preparation of NO2 gas. Also give its reactions.
Nitrogen dioxide is prepared by heating a metal nitrate, for example 2 Pb(NO3)2 gives 2 PbO + 4 NO2 + O2, or by reacting copper with concentrated nitric acid, Cu + 4 HNO3 gives Cu(NO3)2 + 2 NO2 + 2 H2O. Its reactions are: with water it gives nitric and nitrous acids, 2 NO2 + H2O gives HNO3 + HNO2; with alkalies it gives nitrite and nitrate; and it acts as a strong oxidising agent, for example oxidising sulphur dioxide to sulphur trioxide.

Q9. How can PCl3 and PCl5 be used for the preparation of other chemical compounds?
Phosphorus trichloride is used to make phosphorus oxychloride, phosphorous acid, and to replace -OH groups by -Cl in organic compounds (for example alcohols to alkyl chlorides). Phosphorus pentachloride is a stronger chlorinating agent: it converts acids to acid chlorides, alcohols to alkyl chlorides, and is used to test for hydroxyl groups (giving HCl fumes). Both are important laboratory and industrial reagents for introducing chlorine into other compounds.

Q10. (i) Ring test for nitrate. (ii) NO2 as oxidising agent. (iii) HNO3 with arsenic and antimony. (iv) Preparation of PCl3. (v) P2O5 as dehydrating agent.
(i) Ring test: to a solution of the nitrate, add freshly prepared ferrous sulphate solution and then concentrated sulphuric acid carefully down the side of the tube; a brown ring of [Fe(NO)]SO4 forms at the junction of the two layers, confirming nitrate. (ii) NO2 is a strong oxidising agent: it oxidises sulphur dioxide to sulphur trioxide, hydrogen sulphide to sulphur, and carbon monoxide to carbon dioxide, itself being reduced to nitric oxide. (iii) With arsenic, concentrated nitric acid gives arsenic acid: As + 5 HNO3 gives H3AsO4 + 5 NO2 + H2O; with antimony it gives antimonic acid and nitrogen dioxide similarly. (iv) PCl3 is prepared by passing dry chlorine through white phosphorus: P4 + 6 Cl2 gives 4 PCl3, or by heating phosphorus with sulphur chloride; it is purified by distillation. (v) P2O5 is a powerful dehydrating agent: it removes water from nitric acid to give N2O5, from organic acids and amides, and it chars paper and sugar by removing the elements of water.

Q11. Complete and balance the chemical equations (i)-(x).
(i) 4 P + 10 NO gives 2 P2O5 + 5 N2. (ii) 2 NO + Cl2 gives 2 NOCl. (iii) H2S + 2 NO gives S + N2O + H2O. (iv) 2 Pb(NO3)2 gives 2 PbO + 4 NO2 + O2. (v) 2 NO2 + H2O gives HNO3 + HNO2. (vi) 2 NO2 + H2SO4 gives NOHSO4 + HNO3. (vii) 2 HNO2 + 2 HI gives 2 NO + I2 + 2 H2O. (viii) HNO2 + NH3 gives N2 + 2 H2O. (ix) 2 HNO2 + CO(NH2)2 gives CO2 + 2 N2 + 3 H2O. (x) KNO3 + H2SO4 gives KHSO4 + HNO3.

Q12. Methods of preparation of phosphorus pentoxide and its reactions.
Phosphorus pentoxide is prepared by burning phosphorus in excess dry oxygen or air: P4 + 5 O2 gives 2 P2O5. It is a white, deliquescent solid that reacts violently with water to give phosphoric acid: P2O5 + 3 H2O gives 2 H3PO4. It is a powerful dehydrating agent: it converts nitric acid to dinitrogen pentoxide, amides to nitriles, and removes water from many organic compounds.

Q13. Discuss the trends in physical properties of group VIA elements.
In group VIA, atomic size and density increase down the group, while melting and boiling points generally increase (oxygen and sulphur are gases/solid with lower values, selenium and tellurium are solids with higher values). Ionization energy and electronegativity decrease down the group, because the outer electrons are farther from the nucleus and more shielded. Metallic character increases down the group: oxygen and sulphur are non-metals, selenium and tellurium are metalloids, and polonium is a metal; catenation and allotropy decrease down the group.

Q4. What is bleaching powder? How is it prepared commercially? Give its uses.
Bleaching powder is calcium chloro-hypochlorite, Ca(OCl)Cl. It is prepared by passing chlorine gas over dry slaked lime, Ca(OH)2. It is used for bleaching cotton, linen and paper, and for disinfecting water. It is also used in the manufacture of chloroform and as an oxidising agent.

Q7(b). Why is HF a weaker acid than HCl?
In water, HF ionises only slightly, while HCl ionises almost completely. The H-F bond is very strong and short, so it is hard to break. HF molecules also associate through strong hydrogen bonding. The small fluoride ion is strongly hydrated, but the bond strength dominates, so HF is weak.

Q11. What are noble gases? Explain their inertness on the basis of their electronic configuration.
Noble gases are the elements of group VIIIA: helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon and radon. Except helium (1s2), all have the stable ns2np6 configuration in the outer shell. Their shells are completely filled, so they have no tendency to gain, lose or share electrons. They therefore have very high ionization energies and remain chemically inert.

Q13(i). What is iodized salt?
Iodized salt is common table salt mixed with a small amount of potassium iodide or iodate. It supplies iodine, which the thyroid gland needs to make its hormones. Lack of iodine causes goitre, a swelling of the thyroid gland. Iodized salt prevents goitre in people living far from the sea.

Q13(v). Which halogen sublimes to violet vapours?
Iodine sublimes on gentle heating to give violet vapours. It passes directly from the solid state to the gaseous state without melting. The vapour condenses back to shining black-violet crystals on cooling. This property is used to purify iodine by sublimation.

Q13(vii). Which halogen is used in water treatment to kill bacteria?
Chlorine is used to disinfect drinking water and swimming pool water. It dissolves in water to form hypochlorous acid, a powerful germicide. Hypochlorous acid kills bacteria and other harmful micro-organisms. Only a small dose is needed, and it also removes bad odours from water.

Q5(a). Discuss the oxides of chlorine.
The oxides of chlorine are: chlorine monoxide, Cl2O; chlorine dioxide, ClO2; dichlorine hexoxide, Cl2O6; and dichlorine heptoxide, Cl2O7. Cl2O is the anhydride of hypochlorous acid, ClO2 is a powerful oxidising and bleaching agent, and Cl2O7 is the anhydride of perchloric acid. All chlorine oxides are strong oxidising agents and are unstable, decomposing readily to chlorine and oxygen.

Q5(b). What are disproportionation reactions? Explain with an example.
A disproportionation reaction is one in which the same element is both oxidised and reduced in a single reaction. For example, chlorine with cold dilute sodium hydroxide gives chloride and hypochlorite: Cl2 + 2 NaOH gives NaCl + NaOCl + H2O, where chlorine (0) goes to -1 and +1. On warming, hypochlorite disproportionates further: 3 ClO- gives 2 Cl- + ClO3-, where chlorine (+1) goes to -1 and +5.

Q6. Discuss the system of nomenclature used for oxyacids of halogens, with examples.
Oxyacids of halogens are named by the oxidation state of the halogen: hypo-...-ous acid for +1,...-ous acid for +3,...-ic acid for +5, and per-...-ic acid for +7. For chlorine: hypochlorous acid, HClO (+1); chlorous acid, HClO2 (+3); chloric acid, HClO3 (+5); perchloric acid, HClO4 (+7). The salts follow the same pattern: hypochlorite, chlorite, chlorate and perchlorate; acid strength increases with oxidation state.

Q7(a). How are halogen acids ionised in water?
Halogen acids ionise in water by donating a proton to water: HX + H2O gives H3O+ + X-. Hydrochloric, hydrobromic and hydroiodic acids ionise almost completely, so they are strong acids. Hydrofluoric acid ionises only slightly, because the H-F bond is very strong and the fluoride ion is heavily hydrated, so HF is a weak acid.

Q8. Arrange in order: (a) increasing acidic character of HClO, HClO2, HClO3, HClO4; (b) increasing oxidising power of F2, Cl2, Br2, I2.
(a) Increasing acidic character: HClO < HClO2 < HClO3 < HClO4, because more oxygen atoms withdraw electrons from the O-H bond, making it easier to lose H+. (b) Increasing oxidising power: I2 < Br2 < Cl2 < F2, because oxidising power (electronegativity and reduction potential) decreases down the group, with fluorine the strongest oxidising agent.

Q9. What happens when bleaching powder reacts with: dilute H2SO4, excess concentrated H2SO4, NH3, HI and CO2?
(a) Alkanes are prepared by: hydrogenation of alkenes and alkynes; Wurtz reaction (alkyl halides with sodium); decarboxylation of sodium salts of acids with soda lime; reduction of alkyl halides; and Grignard reagents with water. (b) (i) Methane to ethane: methane to chloromethane, then Wurtz reaction with sodium gives ethane. (ii) Ethane to methane: ethane to chloroethane, then to ethanol, then oxidised to acetic acid, then to sodium acetate, then decarboxylation with soda lime gives methane. (iii) Acetic acid to ethane: acetic acid reduced with LiAlH4 to ethanol, then converted to bromoethane, then reduced with zinc and acid to ethane. (iv) Methane to nitromethane: methane with concentrated nitric acid at high temperature and pressure gives nitromethane by vapour-phase nitration.

Q10. Discuss the various commercial uses of halogens and their compounds.
Halogens are used as disinfectants and antiseptics (chlorine for water, iodine as tincture), in bleaching (chlorine, bleaching powder), and in making plastics (fluorine in Teflon, chlorine in PVC). Fluorides are used in toothpaste and water fluoridation; bromides in photography and medicines; iodides in iodized salt and thyroid treatment. Halogen compounds are also used as solvents, refrigerants (freons), fire extinguishers (carbon tetrachloride, historically), and in dyes and drugs.

Q12. Write notes on: (i) oxyfluorides of xenon, (ii) applications of noble gases.
(i) Oxyfluorides of xenon are compounds in which xenon is bonded to both oxygen and fluorine, for example XeOF2, XeOF4 and XeO2F2. They are formed by partial hydrolysis of xenon fluorides (for example XeF6 with water gives XeOF4) and are strong oxidising and fluorinating agents. (ii) Applications of noble gases: helium in balloons and for deep-sea divers' breathing mixtures; neon in advertising signs; argon in electric bulbs and welding; krypton and xenon in lamps and lasers; radon (radioactive) in radiotherapy and, historically, in earthquake prediction studies.

Q13(ii,iii,iv,vi,viii,ix). Short questions: freons and Teflon, ion sizes, iodine lustre, antiseptic halogen, earthquake-prediction gas, bactericidal-lamp gas.
(ii) Freons are chlorofluorocarbons (for example CFCl3, CF2Cl2) used as refrigerants and propellants; Teflon is polytetrafluoroethene (PTFE), a non-stick, heat-resistant polymer made from tetrafluoroethene. (iii) Increasing ionic size: F- < Cl- < Br- < I-, because each ion has an extra electron shell down the group. (iv) Iodine has a metallic lustre because its large, easily polarised molecules form shiny, layered crystals that reflect light like a metal surface. (vi) Iodine is used as an antiseptic, as tincture of iodine (iodine in alcohol) for wounds. (viii) Radon is the gas used for earthquake prediction, because radon emission from the ground changes before earthquakes. (ix) Xenon is used in bactericidal lamps, per the chapter's noble-gas uses list.

Q4. How does the electronic configuration of the valence shell affect: (a) binding energy (b) paramagnetism (c) melting points (d) oxidation states?
(a) More unpaired d-electrons give stronger metallic bonding, so binding energy rises to a peak in the middle of a series. (b) Unpaired electrons make the metal paramagnetic; the moment grows with the number of unpaired electrons. (c) Stronger bonding from unpaired electrons also raises melting and boiling points toward the middle. (d) The ns and (n-1)d electrons can both take part in bonding, giving many variable oxidation states.

Q5. Explain: (a) Ligands (b) Coordination sphere (c) Substitutional alloy (d) Central metal atom.
(a) A ligand is an ion or molecule that donates an electron pair to a metal, like NH3, Cl- or CN-. (b) The coordination sphere is the central metal plus its attached ligands, written in square brackets. (c) A substitutional alloy forms when atoms of one metal replace atoms of another in the crystal, like brass. (d) The central metal atom is the metal ion that accepts electron pairs from the ligands in a complex.

Q8(c). How does the process of galvanizing protect iron from rusting?
In galvanizing, iron is coated with a thin layer of zinc. Zinc is more reactive than iron, so it acts as a sacrificial anode. Even if the coating is scratched, zinc corrodes first and iron stays protected. Zinc also forms a basic carbonate layer which seals the surface from air and moisture.

lessons.notes_html:
Q6. Describe the rules for naming coordination complexes and give examples.
Rules for naming coordination complexes: the cation is named before the anion; ligands are named before the central metal, in alphabetical order ignoring numerical prefixes. Anionic ligands end in -o (chloro, cyano, hydroxo), neutral ligands keep their names except aqua (water), ammine (ammonia) and carbonyl. The oxidation state of the central metal is shown in Roman numerals in brackets, and for anionic complexes the metal name ends in -ate (for example hexacyanoferrate). Examples: [Co(NH3)6]Cl3 is hexaamminecobalt(III) chloride; K4[Fe(CN)6] is potassium hexacyanoferrate(II).

Q7. What is the difference between wrought iron and steel? Explain Bessemer's process.
Wrought iron is almost pure iron (0.12-0.25% carbon), soft and malleable, while steel contains 0.25-2.25% carbon and is harder and stronger. Bessemer's process makes steel from pig iron: molten pig iron is placed in a Bessemer converter and a blast of air is blown through it. The air oxidises silicon, manganese and carbon impurities, and the heat of oxidation keeps the metal molten; measured amounts of spiegeleisen (iron-manganese-carbon alloy) are then added to give steel of the required carbon content.

Q8(a,b). (a) Why damaged tin-plated iron rusts quickly. (b) Under what conditions aluminium corrodes.
(a) Damaged tin-plated iron rusts quickly because tin is less reactive than iron: when the coating breaks, iron becomes the anode of a galvanic cell and corrodes faster than unplated iron, while tin acts as the cathode. (b) Aluminium normally resists corrosion because of a protective oxide layer, but it corrodes when that layer is removed by acids, alkalies, chloride solutions (sea water), or contact with a more noble metal, or by mercury salts.

Q9. How are chromate ions converted into dichromate ions?
Chromate ions are converted to dichromate ions by acid: 2 CrO4(2-) + 2 H+ gives Cr2O7(2-) + H2O. The equilibrium is reversed by alkali, which converts dichromate back to chromate. The change is visible: the solution changes from yellow (chromate) to orange (dichromate).

Q10. Describe the preparation of KMnO4 and K2CrO4.
Potassium permanganate is prepared by fusing manganese dioxide with potassium hydroxide in air to give potassium manganate, K2MnO4, which is then oxidised electrolytically (or with chlorine) to KMnO4. Potassium chromate is prepared by roasting chromite ore (FeCr2O4) with sodium carbonate in air to give sodium chromate, which is converted to potassium chromate by adding potassium chloride. Both preparations use oxidation of the lower oxidation state to the higher one, followed by crystallisation.

Q11. Give systematic names to the complexes (a)-(h).
(a) [Fe(CO)5] is pentacarbonyliron(0). (b) [Co(NH3)6]Cl3 is hexaamminecobalt(III) chloride. (c) [Fe(H2O)6]2+ is hexaaquairon(II) ion. (d) Na3[CoF6] is sodium hexafluorocobaltate(III). (e) K2[Cu(CN)4] is potassium tetracyanocuprate(II). (f) K2[PtCl6] is potassium hexachloroplatinate(IV). (g) [Pt(OH)2(NH3)4]SO4 is tetraamminedihydroxidoplatinum(IV) sulphate. (h) [Cr(OH)3(H2O)3] is trihydroxidotriaquachromium(III).

lessons.notes_html:
Q4. How are organic compounds classified? Give a suitable example of each type.
Organic compounds are first divided into acyclic (open chain) and cyclic (closed chain) compounds. Acyclic example: ethane, CH3-CH3, with an open chain of carbon atoms. Cyclic compounds are homocyclic, with only carbon in the ring, like benzene. They are also heterocyclic, with another atom like nitrogen or oxygen in the ring, like pyridine.

Q8. What is meant by a functional group? Name typical functional groups containing oxygen.
A functional group is an atom or group of atoms that gives an organic compound its characteristic properties. Compounds with the same functional group show similar chemical reactions. Oxygen-containing groups are: hydroxyl (-OH) in alcohols, alkoxy (-OR) in ethers. Carbonyl (>C=O) in aldehydes and ketones, and carboxyl (-COOH) in carboxylic acids.

Q9. What is an organic compound? Explain the importance of Wohler's work.
An organic compound is a compound of carbon, usually with hydrogen, oxygen or nitrogen. Earlier chemists believed organic compounds could only be made by living things, the vital force theory. In 1828 Wohler heated ammonium cyanate, an inorganic salt, and obtained urea, an organic compound. This destroyed the vital force theory and opened the laboratory synthesis of organic compounds.

Q10. Write a short note on cracking of hydrocarbons.
Cracking is the breaking of long-chain hydrocarbons into smaller, more useful molecules. It is done by heating heavy fractions strongly in the absence of oxygen, with a catalyst. For example, decane cracks to give octane and ethene. Cracking increases the yield of petrol and provides alkenes for the chemical industry.

Q13. What is orbital hybridization? Explain sp3, sp2 and sp modes of hybridization of carbon.
Hybridization is the mixing of atomic orbitals of similar energy to form new hybrid orbitals. In sp3 hybridization, one s and three p orbitals mix to give four tetrahedral orbitals, as in methane. In sp2 hybridization, one s and two p orbitals give three planar triangular orbitals, as in ethene. In sp hybridization, one s and one p orbital give two linear orbitals, as in ethyne.

lessons.notes_html:
Q5. What are homocyclic and heterocyclic compounds? Give one example of each.
Homocyclic compounds have a ring made of carbon atoms only, for example benzene and cyclohexane. Heterocyclic compounds have a ring containing at least one atom other than carbon, for example pyridine (nitrogen in the ring), furan (oxygen) and thiophene (sulphur). Heterocyclic compounds are very important in biology: the bases of DNA and many drugs are heterocyclic.

Q6. Write the structural formulas of the two possible isomers of C4H10.
The two isomers of C4H10 are n-butane (CH3-CH2-CH2-CH3, a straight chain) and 2-methylpropane (CH3-CH(CH3)-CH3, a branched chain). Both have the same molecular formula but different structures and properties: n-butane boils at about 0 C, while 2-methylpropane boils at about -12 C. They are chain isomers, the simplest example of structural isomerism in alkanes.

Q7. Why is ethene an important industrial chemical?
Ethene is an important industrial chemical because it is the raw material for many products. It is polymerised to polythene (plastics, bags, bottles), hydrated to ethyl alcohol, and converted to ethylene glycol (antifreeze, polyester) and to chloroethene (PVC). It is also used to ripen fruits artificially and to make ethylene oxide, acetaldehyde and many other chemicals.

Q11. Explain reforming of petroleum with a suitable example.
Reforming is the conversion of straight-chain hydrocarbons of low octane number into branched-chain and aromatic hydrocarbons of high octane number, using heat and a catalyst (platinum). For example, n-heptane (octane number 0) is reformed to toluene, an aromatic compound with a high octane number, by cyclisation and dehydrogenation. Reforming raises the quality of petrol and reduces engine knocking.

Q12. Describe important sources of organic compounds.
The important sources of organic compounds are coal, petroleum and natural gas, which supply most hydrocarbons and their derivatives. Plants and animals supply sugars, starch, cellulose, fats, proteins and natural rubber. Many organic compounds are now also made synthetically in the laboratory and industry, for example urea, dyes, plastics and drugs, from simple starting materials.

Q14. Explain the type of bonds and shapes of CH3-CH3, CH2=CH2, CH triple CH, HCHO and CH3Cl using hybridisation.
Ethane: each carbon is sp3 hybridised, forming four sigma bonds in a tetrahedral shape (bond angle about 109.5 degrees). Ethene: each carbon is sp2 hybridised, forming three sigma bonds in a plane (about 120 degrees) plus one pi bond, giving a planar molecule. Ethyne: each carbon is sp hybridised, forming two sigma bonds in a line (180 degrees) plus two pi bonds, giving a linear molecule. Formaldehyde (HCHO): carbon is sp2 hybridised, trigonal planar. Chloromethane (CH3Cl): carbon is sp3 hybridised, tetrahedral.

Q15. Why is there no free rotation around a double bond and free rotation around a single bond? Discuss cis-trans isomerism.
There is free rotation around a single (sigma) bond because the sigma bond is cylindrically symmetrical about the bond axis, so rotation does not break it. There is no free rotation around a double bond because rotation would break the pi bond, which needs the p orbitals to stay parallel; breaking it costs much energy. This restricted rotation gives cis-trans isomerism in alkenes: when the same groups are on the same side of the double bond it is cis, and when on opposite sides it is trans, provided each double-bond carbon carries two different groups.

Q6. What are the rules for naming alkanes? Explain with suitable examples.
First, select the longest continuous carbon chain as the parent chain. Second, number the chain so that the substituents get the lowest possible numbers. Third, name substituents alphabetically, with their position numbers, like 2-methylbutane. If the same substituent occurs twice, use di, tri, as in 2,2-dimethylpropane.

Q8(a). Explain why alkanes are less reactive than alkenes. What is the effect of branching on the melting point of alkanes?
Alkanes contain only strong C-C and C-H sigma bonds, which are hard to break. Alkenes contain a pi bond, which is weaker and easily attacked by electrophiles. So alkanes are less reactive and undergo substitution only under special conditions. Branching makes molecules more compact, so they pack better and their melting points rise.

Q4. Write the structural formula (in words) for each compound (i)-(viii).
In words: (i) 2-methylpropane is CH3-CH(CH3)-CH3. (ii) Neopentane is the same as 2,2-dimethylpropane, C(CH3)4. (iii) 3-Ethylpentane is CH3-CH2-CH(C2H5)-CH2-CH3. (iv) 4-Ethyl-3,4-dimethylheptane is a 7-carbon chain with an ethyl group at carbon 4 and methyl groups at carbons 3 and 4. (v) 2,2,3,4-Tetramethylpentane is a 5-carbon chain with two methyls at carbon 2 and one each at carbons 3 and 4. (vi) 4-Isopropylheptane is a 7-carbon chain with an isopropyl group at carbon 4. (vii) 2,2-Dimethylbutane is CH3-C(CH3)2-CH2-CH3. (viii) 2,2-Dimethylpropane is C(CH3)4.

Q5. Names by IUPAC system.
Text-given items: (ii) (CH3)3C-CH2-C(CH3)3 is 2,2,4,4-tetramethylpentane. (v) CH3CH2C(CH3)2CH(CH2CH3)CH3 is 3,3-dimethylhexane. (vi) (CH3CH2)3CH is 3-ethylpentane. (vii) CH3C(CH3)2(CH2)2CH3 is 2,2-dimethylpentane. (viii) (C6H5)3CH is triphenylmethane. Diagram items, read from book p.45: (i) CH3-CH2-CH(C2H5)-CH2-CH3 is 3-ethylpentane. (iii) CH3-CH(CH3)-CH2-CH(CH3)2 is 2,4-dimethylpentane. (iv) (CH3)2CH-CH(CH3)-CH(CH3)2 is 2,3,4-trimethylpentane.

Q7. (a) Structural formulas (in words) for all isomeric hexanes. (b) Correct the incorrect IUPAC names.
The isomeric hexanes are: n-hexane (CH3CH2CH2CH2CH2CH3); 2-methylpentane; 3-methylpentane; 2,2-dimethylbutane; and 2,3-dimethylbutane. (b) Correct names: (i) 4-methylpentane is incorrect because the longest chain is 5 carbons numbered to give the methyl the lowest locant: it is 2-methylpentane. (ii) 3,5,5-Trimethylhexane is incorrect: the longest chain is 7 carbons, giving 2,2,4-trimethylheptane. (iii) 2-Methyl-3-ethylbutane is incorrect: the longest chain is 5 carbons, giving 3-methylpentane.

Q8(b). Three different unsaturated compounds yield 2-methylbutane when they are hydrogenated. Give their structures and write equations for the reactions involved.
(b) Three different alkenes give 2-methylbutane on hydrogenation: 2-methyl-1-butene, 2-methyl-2-butene and 3-methyl-1-butene. Each adds one molecule of hydrogen across its double bond over a metal catalyst to give the same saturated product, 2-methylbutane. This shows that hydrogenation removes the double bond but keeps the carbon skeleton, so different double-bond positions give the same alkane.

Q9. (a) Methods of preparation of alkanes. (b) Conversions: methane to ethane, ethane to methane, acetic acid to ethane, methane to nitromethane.
(a) Alkanes are prepared by: hydrogenation of alkenes and alkynes; Wurtz reaction (alkyl halides with sodium); decarboxylation of sodium salts of acids with soda lime; reduction of alkyl halides; and Grignard reagents with water. (b) (i) Methane to ethane: methane to chloromethane, then Wurtz reaction with sodium gives ethane. (ii) Ethane to methane: ethane to chloroethane, then to ethanol, then oxidised to acetic acid, then to sodium acetate, then decarboxylation with soda lime gives methane. (iii) Acetic acid to ethane: acetic acid reduced with LiAlH4 to ethanol, then converted to bromoethane, then reduced with zinc and acid to ethane. (iv) Methane to nitromethane: methane with concentrated nitric acid at high temperature and pressure gives nitromethane by vapour-phase nitration.

Q10. (a) Octane number and knocking. (b) Free radical mechanism of chlorine with methane in sunlight.
(a) Octane number is a measure of a fuel's resistance to knocking (premature explosion) in an engine, rated against iso-octane (100) and n-heptane (0). A high-octane fuel burns smoothly and evenly, so it has less tendency to knock, because it resists auto-ignition under compression. (b) Free radical mechanism for chlorine with methane in sunlight: initiation: Cl2 splits into two chlorine free radicals by sunlight. Propagation: a chlorine radical removes hydrogen from methane to give methyl radical and HCl; the methyl radical reacts with Cl2 to give chloromethane and a new chlorine radical. Termination: two radicals combine, for example two methyl radicals give ethane, or a methyl and a chlorine radical give chloromethane, ending the chain.

Q11. (a) Structural formulas (in words) for (i)-(xii). (b) IUPAC names.
(a) In words: (i) isobutylene is (CH3)2C=CH2 (2-methylpropene). (ii) 2,3,4,4-Tetramethyl-2-pentene is a 5-carbon chain with a double bond at carbon 2 and methyls at 2, 3, 4 and 4. (iii) 2,5-Heptadiene is a 7-carbon chain with double bonds at carbons 2 and 5. (iv) 4,5-Dimethyl-2-hexene is a 6-carbon chain with a double bond at carbon 2 and methyls at 4 and 5. (v) Vinylacetylene is CH2=CH-C triple CH (but-1-en-3-yne). (vi) 1,3-Pentadiene is CH2=CH-CH=CH-CH3. (vii) 1-Butyne is CH triple C-CH2-CH3. (viii) 3-n-Propyl-1,4-pentadiene is a 5-carbon chain with double bonds at 1 and 4 and a propyl group at carbon 3. (ix) Vinyl bromide is CH2=CH-Br. (x) But-1-en-3-yne is CH2=CH-C triple CH. (xi) 4-Methyl-2-pentyne is CH3-C triple C-CH(CH3)-CH3 with the triple bond at carbon 2. (xii) Isopentane is 2-methylbutane. (b) Text-given items: (i) CH3-CH=CH-(CH2)2CH3 is hex-2-ene. (ii) (CH3)2C=CH2 is 2-methylpropene. (iii) The compound with a propyl chain and an isopropyl group on the double-bond carbon is 2-isopropylpent-1-ene. (v) CH2=C(C2H5)CH2CH2CH3 is 2-ethylpent-1-ene. (vi) CH triple C-CH3 is propyne. (ix) CH triple C-CH=CH-C triple CH is hex-3-en-1,5-diyne. (x) CH2=CH-C triple CH is but-1-en-3-yne. Diagram items, read from book p.46: (iv) CH2=CH-CH=CH2 is buta-1,3-diene. (vii) CH3-C triple C-CH3 is but-2-yne. (viii) CH2=CH-C triple C-CH=CH2 is hexa-1,5-dien-3-yne.

Q12. (a) Preparation of alkenes; proof of the double bond in ethylene. (b) Dehydrohalogenation products.
(a) Alkenes are prepared by: dehydration of alcohols with concentrated sulphuric acid; dehydrohalogenation of alkyl halides with alcoholic KOH; hydrogenation of alkynes with Lindlar's catalyst; and cracking of alkanes. Ethylene contains a double bond, proved because it decolourises bromine water (addition) and cold dilute alkaline KMnO4, Baeyer's reagent (hydroxylation to a diol), while ethane does not. (b) Dehydrohalogenation with a strong base: (i) 1-chloropentane gives pent-1-ene. (ii) 2-Chloro-3-methylbutane gives mainly 2-methylbut-2-ene (Saytzeff product) and some 2-methylbut-1-ene. (iii) 1-Chloro-2,2-dimethylpropane (neopentyl chloride) gives 2-methylbut-2-ene by rearrangement, because the primary carbocation rearranges to the more stable tertiary carbocation before losing a proton.

Q13. (a) Preparation of propene. (b) All possible alkenes of formula C5H10 (in words).
(a) Propene from: (i) propan-1-ol by dehydration with concentrated H2SO4; (ii) propyne by partial hydrogenation with Lindlar's catalyst; (iii) isopropyl chloride by dehydrohalogenation with alcoholic KOH. (b) Skeleton formulas in words for C5H10 alkenes: pent-1-ene, pent-2-ene (cis and trans), 2-methylbut-1-ene, 2-methylbut-2-ene, 3-methylbut-1-ene, and cyclopentane (a cycloalkane isomer).

Q14. (a) Ethene to ethyl alcohol. (b) From ethene: 1,2-dibromoethane, ethyne, ethane, ethylene glycol. (c) Conversions.
(a) Ethene is converted to ethyl alcohol by hydration with steam over a phosphoric acid catalyst at high temperature and pressure, or via ethyl hydrogen sulphate with concentrated sulphuric acid followed by hydrolysis. (b) From ethene: (i) with bromine, 1,2-dibromoethane; (ii) 1,2-dibromoethane with alcoholic KOH gives ethyne; (iii) ethene with hydrogen over nickel gives ethane; (iv) ethene with cold dilute alkaline KMnO4 gives ethylene glycol. (c) (i) 1-Butene to 1-butyne: 1-butene with bromine gives 1,2-dibromobutane, then with alcoholic KOH (twice) gives but-1-yne. (ii) 1-Propanol to the chloro compound printed as CH3-CH-CH2Cl: 1-propanol with PCl5 or SOCl2 gives 1-chloropropane, CH3-CH2-CH2Cl (the printed line compresses the middle CH2; no branch substituent is shown on the render).

Q15. Cycle of changes: ethane, ethene, ethyne.
Cycle, in words: Ethane gives ethene by dehydrogenation (heating with a catalyst). Ethene gives ethyne in two steps: ethene with bromine gives 1,2-dibromoethane, and 1,2-dibromoethane with alcoholic KOH (twice) gives ethyne. Ethyne gives ethane back by hydrogenation with hydrogen over a nickel catalyst (ethyne + 2H2 gives ethane), closing the cycle.

Q16. Structural formulas (in words) for the products of 1-butene with the reagents listed.
(i) With H2/Pt, 1-butene gives butane. (ii) With Br2 in CCl4, it gives 1,2-dibromobutane. (iii) With cold dilute KMnO4/OH-, it gives butane-1,2-diol. (iv) With HBr, it gives mainly 2-bromobutane (Markovnikov addition). (v) With O2 in the presence of silver, it gives 1,2-epoxybutane. (vi) With HOCl, it gives 2-chlorobutan-1-ol (chlorohydrin, OH on carbon 1, Cl on carbon 2 by Markovnikov orientation of Cl+). (vii) With dilute H2SO4, it gives mainly butan-2-ol.

Q17. Identify each lettered product (A-F).
(i) Ethyl alcohol with concentrated H2SO4 gives ethene (A); ethene with bromine gives 1,2-dibromoethane (B); B with alcoholic KOH gives ethyne (C). (ii) Propene with bromine gives 1,2-dibromopropane (D); D with alcoholic KOH gives propyne (E); E with HCN gives 2-cyanopropene (F), by Markovnikov addition of HCN across the triple bond.

Q18. After ozonolysis the only product was acetaldehyde. Guess the structural formula.
Ozonolysis of an alkene breaks the double bond and gives carbonyl compounds from each side. If the only product is acetaldehyde, CH3CHO, then both sides of the double bond gave acetaldehyde, so the alkene was symmetric with CH3-CH= on both sides. The compound is therefore but-2-ene, CH3-CH=CH-CH3.

Q19. (a) Alcohols from addition of sulphuric acid to propene, 1-butene, 2-butene. (b) Product of HCl addition to 2-methyl-2-butene.
(a) Addition of sulphuric acid follows Markovnikov's rule (H+ adds to the carbon with more hydrogens, giving the more stable carbocation, then HSO4- adds). (i) Propene gives propan-2-ol (after hydrolysis of isopropyl hydrogen sulphate). (ii) 1-Butene gives butan-2-ol. (iii) 2-Butene gives butan-2-ol. (b) Addition of HCl to 2-methyl-2-butene gives 2-chloro-2-methylbutane: H+ adds to give the tertiary carbocation at carbon 2, which is attacked by Cl-, because the tertiary carbocation is the most stable.

Q20. Why are some hydrocarbons called saturated and others unsaturated? What reactions are characteristic of them?
Hydrocarbons are called saturated when all carbon-carbon bonds are single bonds and each carbon carries the maximum number of hydrogens (alkanes). Unsaturated hydrocarbons contain double or triple bonds (alkenes, alkynes) and have fewer hydrogens than the corresponding alkane. Saturated hydrocarbons characteristically undergo substitution reactions, while unsaturated hydrocarbons characteristically undergo addition reactions across the multiple bond.

Q21(first set). (a) Preparation of ethyne. (b) Reactions of ethyne. (c) Uses of methane, ethene and ethyne.
(a) Ethyne is prepared by: the reaction of calcium carbide with water, CaC2 + 2 H2O gives C2H2 + Ca(OH)2; and by cracking of methane or other hydrocarbons at high temperature. (b) Ethyne reacts: (i) with hydrogen over a catalyst to give ethene and then ethane; (ii) with halogen acids to give vinyl halide and then gem-dihalide (Markovnikov). (iii) With alkaline KMnO4 it is oxidised (the purple colour is discharged, giving oxalic acid and then carbon dioxide). (iv) With 10% H2SO4 and HgSO4 it hydrates to acetaldehyde. (v) With ammoniacal cuprous chloride it gives a red precipitate of copper acetylide, Cu2C2, proving its terminal alkyne character. (c) Uses: methane as a fuel and for making hydrogen, carbon black and chloroform; ethene for polythene, ethanol, ethylene glycol and fruit ripening; ethyne for oxy-acetylene welding and cutting, and for making vinyl chloride, acetaldehyde and acetic acid.

Q21(second set, book p. 49). (a) Identify A and B. (b) General mechanism of electrophilic addition to alkenes.
(a) Propan-1-ol with PCl5 gives 1-chloropropane (A); A with sodium in ether (Wurtz reaction) gives hexane (B): 2 CH3CH2CH2Cl + 2 Na gives CH3(CH2)4CH3 + 2 NaCl. (b) General mechanism of electrophilic addition to alkenes: the pi bond attacks the electrophile (for example H+), forming the more stable carbocation intermediate. The nucleophile (for example Br- or Cl-) then attacks the carbocation, giving the addition product; the orientation follows Markovnikov's rule for unsymmetrical alkenes.

Q22. Distinguish ethane, ethene and ethyne by chemical reactions.
Ethane gives no reaction with bromine water or with ammoniacal cuprous chloride, and does not discharge KMnO4. Ethene decolourises bromine water and alkaline KMnO4, but gives no precipitate with ammoniacal cuprous chloride or silver nitrate. Ethyne decolourises bromine water and KMnO4, and gives a red precipitate with ammoniacal cuprous chloride and a white precipitate with ammoniacal silver nitrate, because it is a terminal alkyne.

Q23. Synthesise from ethyne: acetaldehyde, benzene, chloroprene, glyoxal, oxalic acid, acrylonitrile, ethane, methyl nitrile. (b) Acidity of ethyne.
From ethyne: (i) acetaldehyde by hydration with H2SO4/HgSO4; (ii) benzene by cyclic polymerisation over red-hot iron tube (3 C2H2 gives C6H6). (iii) Chloroprene by addition of HCl to vinylacetylene (itself from ethyne dimerisation); (iv) glyoxal by oxidation of ethyne with nitric acid or by ozonolysis routes. (v) Oxalic acid by oxidation of ethyne; (vi) acrylonitrile by addition of HCN to ethyne; (vii) ethane by complete hydrogenation; (viii) methyl nitrile (acetonitrile) by addition of HCN followed by steps, or from ethyne via acetaldehyde routes in the book's scheme. (b) Ethyne is acidic because its carbon is sp hybridised with 50% s character, so the C-H bond electrons are held close to carbon and the proton is easily lost. Terminal alkynes therefore react with ammoniacal silver nitrate and cuprous chloride to give metal acetylides, while internal alkynes do not.

Q24. (a) Compare reactivity of ethane, ethene and ethyne. (b) Compare physical properties of alkanes, alkenes and alkynes.
(a) Ethane, ethene and ethyne differ in reactivity: ethyne is the most reactive toward electrophilic addition in some contexts, but toward catalytic hydrogenation the order is ethyne > ethene > ethane, because multiple bonds are more reactive than single bonds. In practice, ethene is more reactive than ethyne toward electrophiles because the pi electrons of ethyne are held more tightly (sp hybridisation). (b) Physical properties: alkanes are non-polar, insoluble in water, with boiling points rising with chain length; alkenes are similar but slightly more reactive and with similar boiling points; alkynes have slightly higher boiling points than corresponding alkenes and are also non-polar and water-insoluble.

Q25. How does propyne react with: AgNO3/NH4OH, Cu2Cl2/NH4OH, H2O/H2SO4/HgSO4?
Propyne reacts: (a) with ammoniacal silver nitrate to give a white precipitate of silver propynide (silver acetylide), because it is a terminal alkyne. (b) With ammoniacal cuprous chloride to give a red precipitate of copper propynide. (c) With water, H2SO4 and HgSO4 (hydration, Markovnikov) to give acetone (propanone) via the enol intermediate.

Q26. A compound C4H6, hydrogenated to C4H10, gives a white precipitate with ammoniacal silver nitrate. Identify it.
The compound C4H6 is hydrogenated to C4H10 (butane), so it has two degrees of unsaturation (two double bonds, or one triple bond, or a ring plus a double bond). It gives a white precipitate with ammoniacal silver nitrate, so it is a terminal alkyne. The compound is therefore but-1-yne, CH triple C-CH2-CH3, which hydrogenates to butane and forms silver acetylide.

Cycle of Changes — Ethane, Ethene, Ethyne

lessons.notes_html:
Q4. What are aromatic hydrocarbons? How are they classified?
Aromatic hydrocarbons are benzene and compounds structurally related to benzene. They contain a benzene ring with delocalised pi electrons, which makes them unusually stable. They are classified as monocyclic, like benzene and toluene, and polycyclic, like naphthalene. They may also be benzenoid, containing benzene rings, or non-benzenoid.

Q5(a). What happens when benzene is heated with conc. H2SO4 at 250 C?
At ordinary temperature, benzene gives benzene sulphonic acid by electrophilic substitution. At 250 C with concentrated sulphuric acid, a second sulphonic acid group enters the ring. The product is benzene-1,3-disulphonic acid. The reaction is a sulphonation, and the sulpho group can later be replaced by other groups.

Q5(b). What happens when chlorine is passed through benzene in sunlight?
In sunlight, benzene undergoes free radical addition with chlorine. Three molecules of chlorine add across the ring to give benzene hexachloride. The product is also called gammaxene or BHC, C6H6Cl6. It was once widely used as an insecticide.

Q5(c). What happens when a mixture of benzene vapours and air is passed over heated vanadium pentoxide?
Benzene is oxidised by air over heated V2O5 and the ring is destroyed. The product is maleic acid (maleic anhydride under the reaction conditions). This is catalytic oxidation, unlike the resistance of benzene to KMnO4 or K2Cr2O7 at room temperature.

Q5(d). What happens when benzene is burnt in a free supply of air?
Benzene burns with a smoky flame because of its high carbon content. In a free supply of air it is completely oxidised to carbon dioxide and water. The equation is: 2C6H6 + 15O2 gives 12CO2 + 6H2O. In a limited supply of air, it gives carbon monoxide or soot instead.

Q6(i). What is meant by the term aromatic?
Aromatic originally meant having a pleasant smell, from the Greek word aroma. In modern chemistry it means a compound containing a benzene ring with delocalised pi electrons. Such compounds are unusually stable and undergo electrophilic substitution rather than addition.

Q6(ii). What is meant by oxidation?
Oxidation is a reaction in which a substance loses hydrogen or gains oxygen. For benzene, ordinary oxidising agents do not attack the ring at room temperature. Strong heating with air over V2O5 destroys the ring and gives maleic acid.

Q6(iii). What is meant by sulphonation?
Sulphonation is the replacement of a ring hydrogen of benzene by a sulphonic acid group, -SO3H. It is carried out by heating benzene with concentrated or fuming sulphuric acid. The electrophile is sulphur trioxide, SO3, and the product is benzene sulphonic acid.

Q6(iv). What is meant by nitration?
Nitration is the replacement of a ring hydrogen by a nitro group, -NO2. Benzene is nitrated with a mixture of concentrated nitric and sulphuric acids. The active nitrating agent is the nitronium ion, NO2+.

Q6(v). What is meant by halogenation?
Halogenation is the introduction of a halogen atom into the benzene ring. It is an electrophilic substitution, carried out with Cl2 or Br2 in the presence of a Lewis acid catalyst. The product keeps the aromatic ring, with one hydrogen replaced by the halogen.
