Q7(a). Draw structural formulas for: (i) m-chlorobenzoic acid, (ii) p-hydroxybenzoic acid, (iii) o-bromonitrobenzene, (iv) o-ethyltoluene, (v) p-nitroaniline, (vi) 2,4,6-trinitrotoluene, (vii) m-nitrophenol, (viii) p-dibenzylbenzene, (ix) 2-amino-5-bromo-3-nitrobenzenesulphonic acid.
In each case the benzene ring carries the named groups at the stated positions. (i) -COOH at position 1 and -Cl at position 3. (ii) -COOH at 1 and -OH at 4. (iii) -Br at 1 and -NO2 at 2. (iv) -CH3 at 1 and -C2H5 at 2. (v) -NH2 at 1 and -NO2 at 4. (vi) -CH3 at 1 with -NO2 at 2, 4 and 6. (vii) -OH at 1 and -NO2 at 3. (viii) -CH2C6H5 groups at 1 and 4. (ix) -SO3H at 1, -NH2 at 2, -NO2 at 3 and -Br at 5.

Q7(b). Give names and the possible isomeric structures of: (i) xylenes, (ii) trimethylbenzene, (iii) bromonitrotoluene.
Xylenes are dimethylbenzenes: o-xylene (1,2-), m-xylene (1,3-) and p-xylene (1,4-dimethylbenzene). Trimethylbenzenes are 1,2,3-, 1,2,4- and 1,3,5-trimethylbenzene (hemimellitene, pseudocumene and mesitylene). Bromonitrotoluenes have -CH3, -Br and -NO2 on one ring in the ten possible relative positions, named by numbering the ring so the substituents get the lowest locants.

Q8. Write IUPAC names of the molecules (book p.37).
(a) 4-bromo-2,6-dimethylbenzaldehyde — the aldehyde carbon is carbon 1, methyl groups at carbons 2 and 6, bromine at carbon 4. (b) 3-bromo-4-ethyltoluene — the methyl group is carbon 1, bromine at carbon 3, ethyl at carbon 4. (c) 2-bromo-4-chloro-6-iodophenol — the hydroxyl group is carbon 1, bromine at carbon 2, chlorine at carbon 4, iodine at carbon 6.

Q9. Give the general mechanism of electrophilic aromatic substitution.
First the electrophile attacks the benzene ring and forms a resonance-stabilised carbocation intermediate, the arenium ion. The ring loses its aromatic stability in this slow, rate-determining step. Then a base removes a proton from the intermediate, the pi system is restored, and the substituted benzene is formed.

Q10(a). Describe the structure of benzene on the basis of (i) atomic orbital treatment and (ii) resonance method.
Atomic orbital treatment: each carbon is sp2 hybridised, forming three sigma bonds in a planar hexagon. The remaining unhybridised 2pz orbital on each carbon overlaps sideways to give a delocalised pi cloud above and below the ring. Resonance method: benzene is a hybrid of two Kekule structures and three Dewar structures, with a resonance energy of 150.5 kJ/mol, so no single structure describes it.

Q10(b). Prove that benzene has a cyclic structure.
Benzene, C6H6, forms only one monosubstituted product, which fits a symmetrical ring and not an open chain. It gives three disubstituted isomers (ortho, meta, para), exactly as a six-membered ring predicts. Ozonolysis gives three molecules of glyoxal, showing three double bonds arranged in a ring.

Q11. Predict the major products of bromination of: (a) toluene, (b) nitrobenzene, (c) bromobenzene, (d) benzoic acid, (e) benzaldehyde, (f) phenol.
Ortho- and para-directing groups give mainly o- and p-bromo products: (a) o- and p-bromotoluene, (c) o- and p-dibromobenzene, (f) o- and p-bromophenol. Meta-directing groups give mainly the m-bromo product: (b) m-bromonitrobenzene, (d) m-bromobenzoic acid, (e) m-bromobenzaldehyde. The directing effect comes from whether the group donates electron density to the ring or withdraws it.

Q12. How will you prepare from benzene in two steps: (a) m-chloronitrobenzene, (b) p-chloronitrobenzene?
For (a), first nitrate benzene to nitrobenzene, then chlorinate: the nitro group is meta-directing, so chlorine enters the meta position. For (b), first chlorinate benzene to chlorobenzene, then nitrate: the chlorine atom is ortho- and para-directing, and the para product is separated from the ortho product. The order of the two steps controls the position, because the first group directs the second.

Q13. Complete the reactions, with conditions (book p.38).
(1) Benzene + hydrogen over a nickel catalyst gives cyclohexane. (2) Benzene + oxygen, burning in a free supply of air, gives carbon dioxide and water. (3) Phenol heated with zinc dust gives benzene (and zinc oxide). (4) Benzenesulphonic acid + steam (superheated steam) gives benzene and sulphuric acid — desulphonation. (5) Benzene + sulphur trioxide in concentrated sulphuric acid (fuming sulphuric acid) gives benzenesulphonic acid.

Q14. Detail three reactions in which benzene behaves as if it is a saturated hydrocarbon and three in which it behaves as if it is unsaturated.
As if saturated, benzene undergoes substitution with the ring intact: nitration to nitrobenzene, sulphonation to benzene sulphonic acid, and halogenation to chlorobenzene or bromobenzene. As if unsaturated, benzene undergoes addition: catalytic hydrogenation to cyclohexane, addition of chlorine in sunlight to benzene hexachloride, and ozonolysis to glyoxal. Addition needs drastic conditions, which shows the extra stability of the aromatic ring.

Q15. What are Friedel-Crafts reactions? Give the mechanism with examples of (i) alkylation and (ii) acylation.
Friedel-Crafts reactions are electrophilic substitutions of benzene catalysed by anhydrous AlCl3. In alkylation, an alkyl halide with AlCl3 gives a carbocation electrophile, which substitutes a ring hydrogen; for example, benzene with CH3Cl and AlCl3 gives toluene. In acylation, an acid chloride with AlCl3 gives an acylium ion electrophile; for example, benzene with CH3COCl and AlCl3 gives acetophenone. In both cases the arenium ion intermediate loses a proton to restore the aromatic ring.

Facts to Remember

  • Monohalo derivatives of alkanes are called alkyl halides.
  • The general formula of alkyl halides is CnH2n+1X.
  • An alkyl group with a partial positive charge on the carbon atom is called a carbocation centre.
  • Alkyl halides undergo nucleophilic substitution reactions with nucleophiles.
  • In tertiary alkyl halides the halogen atom is attached to a carbon which is further attached to three carbon atoms directly.
  • The best method for the preparation of alkyl halides is the reaction of alcohols with inorganic reagents.
  • An alkyl group with a partial positive charge on the carbon atom is called an electrophilic centre.
  • The mechanism is called SN1 if it involves one molecule in the rate-determining step.
  • Molecularity of a reaction is defined as the number of molecules taking part in the reaction.
  • Molecularity of E2 reactions is always two and the reactions show second order kinetics.
  • Wurtz synthesis is useful for the preparation of higher (symmetrical) alkanes.
  • Grignard reagents are prepared by the reaction of magnesium metal with alkyl halides in the presence of dry ether.
  • In secondary alkyl halides, the halogen atom is attached to a carbon which is further attached to two carbon atoms directly. — True.
  • Alcohols react with thionyl chloride in ether as solvent to give alkyl halides. — True.
  • Order of reactivity of alkyl halides for a particular alkyl group is: Iodide > Bromide > Chloride > Fluoride. — True.
  • In SN2 reactions the attacking nucleophile always attacks from the side on which the leaving group is attached. — False.
  • Methyl magnesium iodide on hydrolysis yields ethyl alcohol. — False.
  • Primary, secondary and tertiary amines react with Grignard reagents in the same way. — False.
  • The reactions of secondary alkyl halides may follow both SN1 and SN2 mechanisms. — True.
  • SN1 mechanism is a one stage process involving a simultaneous bond breakage and bond formation. — False.
  • In beta-elimination reactions, the two atoms or groups attached to two adjacent carbon atoms are lost under the influence of an electrophile. — False.
  • The reactivity order of alkyl halides is determined by the strength of carbon-halogen bond. — True.
  • In primary alkyl halides, the halogen atom is attached to a carbon which is further attached to how many carbon atoms? Correct answer: C. One
  • The reactivity order of alkyl halides for a particular alkyl group is: Correct answer: C. Iodide > Bromide > Chloride > Fluoride

  • Grignard reagent is reactive due to: Correct answer: C. the polarity of C-Mg bond

  • Alkyl halides are considered to be very reactive compounds towards nucleophiles, because: Correct answer: B. they have an electrophilic carbon and a good leaving group
  • The rate of E1 reaction depends upon: Correct answer: A. the concentration of substrate

lessons.notes_html:
What are alkyl halides? How are they classified?
Alkyl halides are compounds formed when a hydrogen atom of an alkane is replaced by a halogen. They are classified as primary, secondary or tertiary, according to the carbon holding the halogen. Primary halides have the halogen on a carbon attached to one other carbon. Secondary and tertiary halides have it on carbons attached to two and three carbons respectively.

Why are alkyl halides more reactive than alkanes?
The carbon-halogen bond is polar because the halogen is more electronegative than carbon. The carbon therefore carries a partial positive charge and is attacked by nucleophiles. The halide ion is also a good leaving group, so substitution takes place easily. Alkanes have no polar bond and no leaving group, so they are much less reactive.

Distinguish between SN1 and SN2 reactions.
SN1 is a two-step reaction through a carbocation intermediate, and its rate depends only on the alkyl halide. Tertiary halides favour SN1 because their carbocations are stable. SN2 is a one-step reaction in which the nucleophile attacks from the back side as the halide leaves. Primary halides favour SN2, and the product has inverted configuration.

lessons.title: Long Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Q4. Define alkyl halide. Which is the best method of preparing alkyl halides?
An alkyl halide is a compound formed when a hydrogen atom of an alkane is replaced by a halogen atom. The best method of preparation is the reaction of alcohols with inorganic halides such as SOCl2, PX3 or PX5. These reagents replace -OH by -X cleanly, and the by-products escape as gases or are easily removed.

Q5. Write down a method for the preparation of ethyl magnesium bromide in the laboratory?
Dry ethyl bromide is added to magnesium turnings in dry ether, with stirring and gentle warming to start the reaction. The magnesium inserts into the C-Br bond to give ethyl magnesium bromide, C2H5MgBr, dissolved in ether. Water must be strictly excluded, because water destroys the Grignard reagent by hydrolysis.

Q6. Give IUPAC names to the compounds.
The text-given compounds are named: (iv) 1-chloro-2,2-dimethylpropane, (v) 2-bromopropane, (vi) 1-chloro-2-ethyl-4-methylpentane, (vii) tetrabromomethane, (ix) dichloromethane, (x) 1-bromo-4,4-dimethylpentane, (xiii) 3-bromo-3-ethylpentane. In each name the longest chain containing the halogen is numbered to give the halogen the lowest locant. Diagram items, read from book p.23: (i) CH3-CH(CH3)-CH2-CHCl-CH3 is 2-chloro-4-methylpentane. (ii) CH3CH2-CH(CH3)-CHBr-CH2CH3 is 3-bromo-4-methylhexane. (iii) (CH3CH2)2CH-CH2-CHCl-CH3 is 2-chloro-4-ethylhexane. (viii) BrCH2-CH2Br is 1,2-dibromoethane. (xi) (CH3)2CH-CH2-CCl(CH3)2 is 2-chloro-2,4-dimethylpentane. (xii) (CH3)2CCl-CCl(CH3)2 is 2,3-dichloro-2,3-dimethylbutane.

Q7. Draw all the possible structures that have the molecular formula C6H13Cl.
Classify each as primary, secondary or tertiary chloride and give IUPAC names. There are 17 structural isomers of C6H13Cl. Primary chlorides: 1-chlorohexane, 1-chloro-2-methylpentane, 1-chloro-4-methylpentane, 1-chloro-3-methylpentane, 1-chloro-2-ethylbutane, 1-chloro-2,2-dimethylbutane, 1-chloro-3,3-dimethylbutane, 1-chloro-2,3-dimethylbutane. Secondary chlorides: 2-chlorohexane, 3-chlorohexane, 3-chloro-2-methylpentane, 2-chloro-4-methylpentane, 2-chloro-3-methylpentane, 3-chloro-2,2-dimethylbutane. Tertiary chlorides: 2-chloro-2-methylpentane, 3-chloro-3-methylpentane, 2-chloro-2,3-dimethylbutane. Classification follows the carbon carrying chlorine: attached to one, two or three other carbons respectively.

Q8. Using ethyl bromide as starting material, prepare: (a) n-butane, (b) ethyl alcohol, (c) ethyl cyanide, (d) ethane, (e) ethene, (f) propanoic acid, (g) propane.
(a) Wurtz reaction: 2 C2H5Br + 2 Na gives n-butane. (b) Aqueous KOH gives ethyl alcohol. (c) KCN gives ethyl cyanide (propanenitrile). (d) Reduction with Zn and acid gives ethane. (e) Alcoholic KOH gives ethene by elimination. (f) KCN followed by hydrolysis of the nitrile gives propanoic acid. (g) Through the Grignard reagent with methyl bromide, C2H5MgBr + CH3Br gives propane.

Q9. Write a detailed note on the mechanism of nucleophilic substitution reactions.
Nucleophilic substitution replaces the halogen of an alkyl halide by a nucleophile. In SN2, the nucleophile attacks from the back side in one step, through a transition state, with inversion of configuration; the rate depends on both reactants. In SN1, the C-X bond first breaks to give a planar carbocation, which is then attacked from either side; the rate depends only on the alkyl halide, and racemisation occurs. Primary halides favour SN2 and tertiary halides favour SN1, while secondary halides may follow either path.

Q10. What do you understand by beta-elimination? Explain briefly the two possible mechanisms.
Beta-elimination removes a hydrogen from the beta carbon and the halogen from the alpha carbon, forming a double bond. In E2, the base removes the beta hydrogen and the leaving group leaves in one concerted step; the rate depends on both substrate and base. In E1, the leaving group first leaves to give a carbocation, and then the base removes a beta hydrogen; the rate depends only on the substrate. E1 and SN1 share the same first step, so they often compete with each other.

Q11. What products are formed when the following are treated with ethyl magnesium bromide followed by acid hydrolysis: (i) HCHO, (ii) CH3CHO, (iii) CO2, (iv) (CH3)2CO, (v) CH3CH2CHO, (vi) ClCN?
Ethyl magnesium bromide adds to the carbonyl carbon, and acid hydrolysis gives the alcohol. (i) HCHO gives propan-1-ol. (ii) CH3CHO gives butan-2-ol. (iii) CO2 gives propanoic acid. (iv) (CH3)2CO gives 2-methylbutan-2-ol. (v) CH3CH2CHO gives pentan-3-ol. (vi) ClCN gives propanenitrile. Formaldehyde gives a primary alcohol, other aldehydes a secondary alcohol, and ketones a tertiary alcohol.

Q12. How will you carry out the following conversions: (i) CH4 to CH3CH2COOH, (ii) CH3CH3 to (CH3CH2)4N+ Br-, (iii) CH2=CH2 to CH3CH2CH2CH2OH, (iv) CH3CH2CH2Cl to CH3CH=CH2, (v) CH3COOH to CH3CH2COOH?
(i) Methane to propanoic acid: CH4 to CH3Cl, then to CH3MgCl, then with formaldehyde to ethanol, then to bromoethane, then to C2H5MgBr, then with CO2 and hydrolysis to propanoic acid. (ii) Ethane to tetraethylammonium bromide: ethane to bromoethane, then stepwise with ammonia to triethylamine, then with bromoethane to (C2H5)4N+ Br-. (iii) Ethene to butan-1-ol: ethene to bromoethane, then to C2H5MgBr, then with ethylene oxide and hydrolysis to butan-1-ol. (iv) 1-Chloropropane to propene: alcoholic KOH causes dehydrohalogenation to propene. (v) Acetic acid to propanoic acid: acetic acid reduced to ethanol, then to bromoethane, then to C2H5MgBr, then with CO2 and hydrolysis to propanoic acid.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Why is phenol more acidic than alcohol?
When phenol loses a proton it forms the phenoxide ion, which is stabilised by resonance. The negative charge is spread over the benzene ring, so the ion is stable. When an alcohol loses a proton, the alkoxide ion has no such resonance stabilisation. Phenol therefore ionises more readily and is a stronger acid than alcohol.

How are alcohols classified? Give one example of each class.
Alcohols are classified by the number of hydroxyl groups: monohydric, dihydric and trihydric. Ethanol is monohydric, ethylene glycol is dihydric and glycerol is trihydric. They are also classified as primary, secondary or tertiary by the carbon holding the OH group. Methanol is primary, isopropyl alcohol is secondary and tertiary butyl alcohol is tertiary.

Why do alcohols have higher boiling points than the corresponding alkanes?
Alcohol molecules are linked by hydrogen bonds between the oxygen of one molecule and the hydrogen of another. These bonds need extra energy to break, so more heat is required to boil the liquid. Alkanes have only weak van der Waals forces between their molecules. Alcohols therefore boil at much higher temperatures than alkanes of similar molar mass.

lessons.title: Long Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Q4. What are alcohols? How are they classified? How will you distinguish between primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols?
Alcohols are hydroxy derivatives of aliphatic hydrocarbons, with general formula R-OH. They are classified as monohydric (one -OH), dihydric (two -OH) and trihydric (three -OH); also as primary, secondary or tertiary by the carbon carrying -OH. Lucas reagent (conc. HCl with ZnCl2) distinguishes them: tertiary alcohols give turbidity at once, secondary after a few minutes, and primary only on heating.

Q5. How is methyl alcohol obtained on a large scale? How may it be distinguished from ethyl alcohol?
Methanol is made on a large scale from water gas: CO + 2 H2 gives CH3OH over a ZnO/Cr2O3 catalyst at high temperature and pressure. Methanol and ethanol are distinguished by the iodoform test: ethanol gives a yellow precipitate of iodoform, methanol does not. Ethanol on oxidation gives acetaldehyde and then acetic acid, while methanol gives formaldehyde and then formic acid.

Q6. What is fermentation? Which compound may be obtained on industrial scale by fermentation?
Fermentation is the breakdown of carbohydrates by microorganisms (yeast) with enzymes, giving alcohol and carbon dioxide. Starch is first converted by diastase to maltose, then by maltase to glucose, and zymase converts glucose to ethyl alcohol and carbon dioxide. Ethyl alcohol is the compound obtained on an industrial scale by fermentation, for example in Pakistan from molasses.

Q7. Explain: absolute alcohol, methylated spirit, rectified spirit, denaturing of alcohols.
Absolute alcohol is almost 100% pure ethyl alcohol, free from water. Rectified spirit is about 95% ethyl alcohol and 5% water, the mixture obtained by ordinary distillation. Methylated spirit is rectified spirit denatured by adding methanol (and a dye) so that it is unfit for drinking. Denaturing means adding a poisonous or bad-tasting substance to alcohol to make it undrinkable.

Q8. How does ethyl alcohol react with: (i) conc. H2SO4, (ii) Na, (iii) PCl5, (iv) CH3COOH, (v) SOCl2?
(i) With concentrated H2SO4 at 170 C, ethyl alcohol dehydrates to ethene; at 140 C it gives diethyl ether. (ii) With sodium it gives sodium ethoxide and hydrogen gas. (iii) With PCl5 it gives chloroethane, POCl3 and HCl. (iv) With acetic acid it gives ethyl acetate (esterification). (v) With SOCl2 it gives chloroethane, SO2 and HCl.

Q9. How will you obtain primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols by reacting Grignard reagent with suitable carbonyl compounds?
A Grignard reagent adds to the carbonyl carbon, and acid hydrolysis gives an alcohol. With formaldehyde it gives a primary alcohol (for example, CH3MgI with HCHO gives ethanol). With any other aldehyde it gives a secondary alcohol, and with a ketone it gives a tertiary alcohol.

Q10. How will you distinguish between: (i) an alcohol and a phenol, (ii) an alcohol and an ether, (iii) methanol and ethanol, (iv) a tertiary alcohol and a primary alcohol, (v) 1-propanol and 2-propanol?
(i) An alcohol gives a neutral ferric chloride test result and no bromine-water precipitate, while phenol gives a violet colour with FeCl3 and a white precipitate of tribromophenol with bromine water. (ii) An alcohol is soluble in water and reacts with sodium, while an ether does not react with sodium and is less soluble. (iii) Methanol gives no iodoform test, while ethanol gives a yellow iodoform precipitate. (iv) A tertiary alcohol gives immediate turbidity with Lucas reagent, while a primary alcohol reacts only on heating. (v) 1-Propanol is a primary alcohol and reacts slowly with Lucas reagent, while 2-propanol is secondary and reacts within minutes.

Q11. Give reasons for: (i) ethyl alcohol is a liquid while methyl chloride is a gas, (ii) ethanol has higher boiling point than diethyl ether, (iii) absolute alcohol cannot be prepared by fermentation, (iv) ethanol gives different products with conc. H2SO4 under different conditions, (v) water has higher boiling point than ethanol.
(i) Ethyl alcohol is a liquid because its molecules are held together by hydrogen bonding, while methyl chloride has no hydrogen bonding and is a gas. (ii) Ethanol has strong hydrogen bonding between its molecules, while diethyl ether molecules cannot hydrogen-bond with each other, so ethanol boils higher. (iii) Fermentation stops when the alcohol concentration reaches about 12%, because higher concentrations kill the yeast; absolute alcohol therefore needs distillation and chemical drying. (iv) With concentrated H2SO4, ethanol gives ethene at 170 C and diethyl ether at 140 C, because temperature controls which dehydration path dominates. (v) Water forms a more extensive hydrogen-bond network than ethanol, since each water molecule can form more hydrogen bonds, so water boils higher.

Q12. How will you convert: (i) methanol into ethanol, (ii) ethanol into methanol, (iii) ethanol into isopropyl alcohol, (iv) formaldehyde into ethyl alcohol, (v) acetone into ethyl alcohol?
(i) Methanol to ethanol: methanol to iodomethane, then to the Grignard reagent, then with formaldehyde and hydrolysis to ethanol. (ii) Ethanol to methanol: ethanol oxidised to acetic acid, then decarboxylated with soda lime to methane, then chlorinated to chloromethane, then hydrolysed with aqueous KOH to methanol. (iii) Ethanol to isopropyl alcohol: ethanol oxidised to acetaldehyde, then reacted with methylmagnesium iodide and hydrolysed to propan-2-ol. (iv) Formaldehyde to ethyl alcohol: formaldehyde with methylmagnesium iodide, then hydrolysis, gives ethanol. (v) Acetone to ethyl alcohol: acetone undergoes the haloform reaction to give acetate, acidified to acetic acid, then reduced with LiAlH4 to ethanol.

Q13. Explain using ethyl alcohol as example: (i) oxidation, (ii) dehydration, (iii) esterification, (iv) ether formation.
(i) Oxidation: ethyl alcohol oxidised with acidified K2Cr2O7 gives acetaldehyde, and further oxidation gives acetic acid. (ii) Dehydration: with concentrated H2SO4 at 170 C it gives ethene, and at 140 C it gives diethyl ether. (iii) Esterification: with acetic acid in the presence of concentrated H2SO4 it gives ethyl acetate and water. (iv) Ether formation: two molecules of ethyl alcohol with concentrated H2SO4 at 140 C give diethyl ether and water.

Q14. Compare the reactions of phenol with those of ethanol. Discuss the difference, if any.
Phenol is more acidic than ethanol because the phenoxide ion is stabilised by resonance over the benzene ring, while the ethoxide ion is not. Phenol reacts with NaOH to give sodium phenoxide, while ethanol does not react with aqueous NaOH. Phenol gives a violet colour with ferric chloride and a white precipitate with bromine water, while ethanol gives neither test. Both give esters and ethers, but phenol's reactions are those of a weak acid, whereas ethanol behaves as a very weak acid and a neutral alcohol.

Q15. Arrange in order of increasing acid strength and give reasons: H2O, C2H5OH, C6H5OH, C6H5COOH.
Increasing acid strength: C2H5OH < H2O < C6H5OH < C6H5COOH. Ethanol is the weakest acid because the ethoxide ion is not stabilised; water is stronger than ethanol but weaker than phenol. Phenol is stronger than water because the phenoxide ion is resonance-stabilised over the ring. Benzoic acid is the strongest because the carboxylate ion spreads its negative charge equally over two oxygen atoms.

Q16. Write down two methods for preparing phenol. What is the action of HNO3, NaOH, Zn and bromine water on phenol?
Phenol is prepared by the Dow process (chlorobenzene with NaOH at high temperature and pressure, then acidification) and by fusion of sodium benzene sulphonate with NaOH followed by acidification. With concentrated HNO3 it gives picric acid (2,4,6-trinitrophenol). With NaOH it gives sodium phenoxide. With zinc dust it is reduced to benzene. With bromine water it gives a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol.

Q17. Give the uses of phenols. How is bakelite prepared from it?
Phenol is used as an antiseptic and disinfectant, in making bakelite, dyes, drugs and picric acid. Bakelite is prepared by the condensation of phenol with formaldehyde in the presence of an acid or base catalyst. The product is a hard, heat-resistant cross-linked resin used for electrical fittings and handles.

Q18. (a) Write IUPAC names of the compounds given. (b) Write structure formulas in words for: glycol, glycerol, carbolic acid, acetophenone, picric acid.
(a) (CH3)2CH-OH is propan-2-ol. (CH3)2CHCH2OH is 2-methylpropan-1-ol. (CH3)3COH is 2-methylpropan-2-ol. C2H5-CH(OH)-CH3 is butan-2-ol. (b) In words: glycol is HO-CH2-CH2-OH; glycerol is HO-CH2-CH(OH)-CH2-OH; carbolic acid is C6H5-OH; acetophenone is C6H5-CO-CH3; picric acid is 2,4,6-trinitrophenol.

Q19. (a) Name the ethers given. (b) Write down structural formulas in words for: methoxyethane, ethoxybenzene, sodium ethoxide, sodium phenoxide, propoxypropane.
(a) CH3-CH2-CH2-O-CH3 is 1-methoxypropane. C6H5-O-C6H5 is diphenyl ether (phenoxybenzene). (CH3)2CH-O-CH(CH3)2 is diisopropyl ether (2-propoxypropane). CH3-O-C6H5 is methoxybenzene (anisole). CH3-CH2-CH2-O-CH2-CH3 is 1-ethoxypropane. (b) In words: methoxyethane is CH3-O-CH2-CH3; ethoxybenzene is C6H5-O-C2H5; sodium ethoxide is C2H5-ONa; sodium phenoxide is C6H5-ONa; propoxypropane is CH3-CH2-CH2-O-CH2-CH2-CH3.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Distinguish between aldehydes and ketones.
An aldehyde has the carbonyl group at the end of the chain, bonded to at least one hydrogen. A ketone has the carbonyl group in the middle, bonded to two carbon groups. Aldehydes are easily oxidised to carboxylic acids, while ketones resist oxidation. Aldehydes give a silver mirror with Tollens reagent, but ketones do not.

Why is the carbonyl carbon attacked by nucleophiles?
Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so the C=O bond is polar. The carbonyl carbon carries a partial positive charge. Nucleophiles, which are electron-rich, are attracted to this positive centre. Addition of the nucleophile to the carbon is therefore the characteristic reaction of carbonyl compounds.

lessons.notes_html:
Q4. Give one laboratory and one industrial method for the preparation of formaldehyde.
Laboratory method: oxidation of methanol vapour with air over a heated platinum or copper catalyst gives formaldehyde. Industrial method: methanol and air are passed over a silver catalyst at high temperature, giving formaldehyde on a large scale. Formaldehyde is collected as an aqueous solution, formalin.

Q5. How does formaldehyde react with: (i) CH3MgI, (ii) HCN, (iii) NaHSO3, (iv) conc.
NaOH, (v) NaBH4/H2O, (vi) Tollen's reagent, (vii) Fehling's reagent? (i) CH3MgI, then hydrolysis: gives ethanol (a primary alcohol). (ii) HCN: gives formaldehyde cyanohydrin, hydroxymethanenitrile. (iii) NaHSO3: gives a white crystalline addition product, used to purify aldehydes. (iv) Concentrated NaOH: Cannizzaro reaction gives methanol and sodium formate. (v) NaBH4/H2O: reduces formaldehyde to methanol. (vi) Tollen's reagent: gives a silver mirror. (vii) Fehling's solution: gives a red precipitate of Cu2O.

Q6. Give one laboratory and one industrial method for the preparation of acetaldehyde.
Laboratory method: oxidation of ethyl alcohol with acidified potassium dichromate gives acetaldehyde, distilled off as it forms. Industrial method: hydration of ethyne with dilute H2SO4 and HgSO4 catalyst gives acetaldehyde. The Wacker process (oxidation of ethene with PdCl2/CuCl and oxygen) is another industrial route to acetaldehyde.

Q7. How does acetaldehyde react with: (i) C2H5MgI, (ii) HCN, (iii) NaHSO3, (iv) dilute NaOH, (v) I2/NaOH, (vi) NaBH4/H2O, (vii) NH2OH, (viii) K2Cr2O7/H2SO4?
(i) C2H5MgI, then hydrolysis: gives butan-2-ol. (ii) HCN: gives acetaldehyde cyanohydrin (2-hydroxypropanenitrile). (iii) NaHSO3: gives a white crystalline bisulphite addition compound. (iv) Dilute NaOH: aldol condensation gives 3-hydroxybutanal (aldol). (v) I2/NaOH: gives yellow iodoform precipitate. (vi) NaBH4/H2O: reduces acetaldehyde to ethanol. (vii) NH2OH: gives acetaldoxime. (viii) K2Cr2O7/H2SO4: oxidises acetaldehyde to acetic acid.

Q8. Describe briefly the mechanism of nucleophilic addition to a carbonyl compound.
The carbonyl carbon is electrophilic because oxygen pulls electrons away from it. The nucleophile attacks the carbonyl carbon, and the pi bond electrons move to oxygen, giving a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate. Protonation of the alkoxide oxygen gives the addition product, an alcohol derivative.

Q9. Explain with mechanism the addition of ethylmagnesium bromide to acetaldehyde. What is the importance of this reaction?
Ethylmagnesium bromide attacks the carbonyl carbon of acetaldehyde, giving a magnesium alkoxide intermediate. Acid hydrolysis protonates the alkoxide to give butan-2-ol, a secondary alcohol. The reaction is important because it forms a new carbon-carbon bond and lengthens the carbon chain by two carbons.

Q10. Explain with mechanism the addition of sodium bisulphite to acetone. What is the utility of this reaction?
The bisulphite ion attacks the carbonyl carbon of acetone, giving a white crystalline addition compound, acetone sodium bisulphite. Acid or base treatment of the addition compound regenerates acetone. The reaction is useful for purifying and identifying aldehydes and small ketones, since the addition compound can be filtered and then decomposed.

Q11. Describe with mechanism aldol condensation. Why does formaldehyde not give this reaction?
In the presence of dilute base, one acetaldehyde molecule forms an enolate ion, which attacks the carbonyl carbon of a second molecule. The product after protonation is 3-hydroxybutanal, called aldol, which has both an alcohol and an aldehyde group. Formaldehyde does not give this reaction because it has no alpha-hydrogen atom, so it cannot form an enolate ion.

Q12. What types of aldehydes give Cannizzaro's reaction? Give its mechanism.
Aldehydes with no alpha-hydrogen atom give Cannizzaro's reaction, for example formaldehyde and benzaldehyde. With concentrated alkali, one molecule is oxidised to the carboxylic acid salt and another is reduced to the alcohol. The mechanism involves hydride transfer from one aldehyde molecule to another, through a tetrahedral intermediate formed by hydroxide attack.

Q13. Explain the mechanism of the reaction of phenylhydrazine with acetone.
Phenylhydrazine attacks the carbonyl carbon of acetone as a nucleophile, giving a tetrahedral intermediate. Loss of water from the intermediate gives acetone phenylhydrazone, (CH3)2C=N-NH-C6H5. The reaction is a condensation: the carbonyl oxygen is lost as water and a C=N double bond is formed.

Q14. Using ethyne as starting material, how would you get acetaldehyde, acetone and ethyl alcohol?
Ethyne hydrated with dilute H2SO4 and HgSO4 gives acetaldehyde. Acetaldehyde reduced with NaBH4 or H2 gives ethyl alcohol. Acetaldehyde oxidised to acetic acid, converted to calcium acetate, and dry-distilled gives acetone; so all three products come from ethyne through acetaldehyde.

Q15. Give the mechanism of addition of HCN to acetone.
Cyanide ion attacks the carbonyl carbon of acetone, giving a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate. Protonation of the alkoxide gives acetone cyanohydrin, (CH3)2C(OH)CN. The reaction is catalysed by base, which generates the cyanide nucleophile from HCN.

Q16. How would you bring about the conversions listed in the book (i)-(xii)?
(i) Acetone to t-butyl alcohol: acetone with CH3MgI, then hydrolysis, gives 2-methylpropan-2-ol. (ii) Propanal to 1-propanol: reduction with NaBH4 gives propan-1-ol. (iii) Propanone to 2-propanol: reduction with NaBH4 gives propan-2-ol. (iv) Methanal to ethanal: methanal with CH3MgI, then hydrolysis, gives ethanol; oxidation of ethanol gives ethanal. (v) Ethanal to propanone: ethanal oxidised to acetic acid, converted to calcium acetate, dry-distilled to acetone. (vi) Ethanal to 2-propanol: ethanal with CH3MgI, then hydrolysis, gives propan-2-ol. (vii) Ethyne to ethanal: hydration of ethyne with H2SO4/HgSO4 gives ethanal. (viii) Ethene to ethanal: ethene oxidised by the Wacker process gives ethanal. (ix) Ethanal to ethanol: reduction with NaBH4 gives ethanol. (x) Ethanol to 2-butanone: ethanol oxidised to ethanal, then Grignard with C2H5MgI gives butan-2-ol, oxidised to butanone. (xi) Methanol to ethanal: methanol to iodomethane, then Grignard with formaldehyde gives ethanol, oxidised to ethanal. (xii) Ethanol to ethanoic acid: oxidation with acidified K2Cr2O7 gives ethanoic acid.

Q17. How will you distinguish between the pairs listed in the book (i)-(vii)?
(i) Methanal and ethanal: ethanal gives iodoform with I2/NaOH, methanal does not. (ii) Ethanal and propanone: ethanal gives a silver mirror with Tollen's reagent, propanone does not. (iii) Ethanal and propanal: ethanal gives iodoform, propanal does not. (iv) Acetone and ethyl alcohol: acetone gives iodoform, ethyl alcohol also gives iodoform, but acetone does not react with sodium while ethyl alcohol liberates hydrogen. (v) Butanone and 3-pentanone: butanone gives iodoform, 3-pentanone does not. (vi) Acetaldehyde and benzaldehyde: acetaldehyde gives iodoform and aldol reaction, benzaldehyde gives neither but gives Cannizzaro reaction. (vii) 2-Pentanone and 3-pentanone: 2-pentanone gives iodoform, 3-pentanone does not.

Q18. Discuss oxidation of (a) aldehydes and (b) ketones with: (i) K2Cr2O7/H2SO4, (ii) Tollen's reagent, (iii) Fehling's solution.
With K2Cr2O7/H2SO4, aldehydes are oxidised to carboxylic acids, while ketones resist oxidation except under drastic conditions where the chain breaks. With Tollen's reagent, aldehydes give a silver mirror, while ketones give no reaction. With Fehling's solution, aldehydes give a red precipitate of Cu2O, while ketones give no reaction.

Q19. Discuss reduction of (a) aldehydes and (b) ketones with: (i) NaBH4/H2O, (ii) H2/Pd.
With NaBH4/H2O, aldehydes are reduced to primary alcohols and ketones to secondary alcohols. With H2/Pd, aldehydes are reduced to primary alcohols and ketones to secondary alcohols, under catalytic hydrogenation conditions. Sodium borohydride is a selective reagent: it reduces the carbonyl group but leaves most other groups untouched.

Q20. Give three uses for each of formaldehyde and acetaldehyde.
Formaldehyde uses: as formalin for preserving biological specimens, as a disinfectant, and in making bakelite and other resins. Acetaldehyde uses: in making acetic acid and acetic anhydride, in making resins and dyes, and as an intermediate for alcohols and acids. Formaldehyde is also used in silvering mirrors, and acetaldehyde in the manufacture of chloral and paraldehyde.

Why are carboxylic acids stronger acids than alcohols and phenols?
A carboxylic acid loses a proton to give a carboxylate ion. The negative charge in the carboxylate ion is shared equally by two oxygen atoms through resonance. This makes the ion very stable, so the acid ionises readily. Alkoxide and phenoxide ions are less stabilised, so alcohols and phenols are weaker acids.

Why do carboxylic acids have high boiling points?
Carboxylic acid molecules form strong hydrogen bonds with each other. Two molecules pair up as a dimer, held by two hydrogen bonds. Breaking these bonds needs much energy, so the boiling point is high. They therefore boil higher than alcohols and aldehydes of similar molar mass.

In words: (i) valeric acid is CH3-CH2-CH2-CH2-COOH. (ii) Propionic acid is CH3-CH2-COOH. (iii) Oxalic acid is HOOC-COOH. (iv) Benzoic acid is C6H5-COOH. (v) Acetic anhydride is (CH3CO)2O. (vi) Acetyl chloride is CH3-CO-Cl.

Q5. IUPAC names (book p.26). (v)-(vi) Write down the names by IUPAC system of the text-given compounds.
(i) CH2(COOH)2 is propanedioic acid (malonic acid). (ii) Benzene-1,3-dicarboxylic acid (isophthalic acid) — carboxyl groups at carbons 1 and 3. (iii) H-COOH is methanoic acid (formic acid). (iv) CH3-COO-C2H5 is ethyl ethanoate (ethyl acetate). (v) and (vi) are named in the next item. (v) NH2-CH2-COOH is glycine (aminoethanoic acid). (vi) HCOO-C3H7 is propyl methanoate (propyl formate). Glycine is the simplest amino acid, and propyl formate is an ester of formic acid with propyl alcohol.

Q6. (a) How is acetic acid manufactured? What is glacial acetic acid? (b) How would you convert acetic acid into: (i) methane, (ii) acetyl chloride, (iii) acetamide, (iv) acetic anhydride?
Acetic acid is manufactured by the fermentation of ethanol (vinegar process) and industrially by oxidation of acetaldehyde or carbonylation of methanol. Glacial acetic acid is pure, anhydrous acetic acid, which freezes to ice-like crystals at about 16.6 C. (b) (i) With soda lime and heat, acetic acid decarboxylates to methane. (ii) With PCl5 or SOCl2 it gives acetyl chloride. (iii) With ammonia it gives ammonium acetate, which on heating gives acetamide. (iv) With P2O5 (dehydration) it gives acetic anhydride.

Q7. (a) What are fatty acids? (b) What is vinegar? Describe how vinegar is prepared from ethanol?
Fatty acids are long-chain aliphatic monocarboxylic acids, usually with an even number of carbon atoms, for example palmitic acid and stearic acid. Vinegar is a dilute (about 5%) aqueous solution of acetic acid. It is prepared from ethanol by fermentation with Acetobacter bacteria, which oxidise ethanol to acetic acid in the presence of air.

Q8. How would you carry out: (i) acetic acid into acetamide, (ii) acetic acid into acetone?
(i) Acetic acid to acetamide: acetic acid with ammonia gives ammonium acetate, which on heating gives acetamide and water. (ii) Acetic acid to acetone: acetic acid converted to calcium acetate, which on dry distillation gives acetone and calcium carbonate. Both conversions use the carboxyl group: one replaces -OH by -NH2, the other removes the carboxyl carbon as carbonate.

Q9. Write down the mechanisms of: (i) acetic acid and ethanol, (ii) acetic acid and ammonia, (iii) acetic acid and thionyl chloride.
(i) Acetic acid with ethanol, acid-catalysed: the alcohol oxygen attacks the carbonyl carbon, water is lost, and ethyl acetate is formed. (ii) Acetic acid with ammonia: ammonium acetate forms first, and heating loses water to give acetamide. (iii) Acetic acid with thionyl chloride: the -OH is replaced by -Cl through a chlorosulphite intermediate, giving acetyl chloride, SO2 and HCl.

Q10. What happens when the following are heated: (i) calcium acetate, (ii) sodium formate and soda lime, (iii) ammonium acetate?
(i) Calcium acetate on heating (dry distillation) gives acetone and calcium carbonate. (ii) Sodium formate with soda lime on heating gives hydrogen gas and sodium carbonate. (iii) Ammonium acetate on heating loses water and gives acetamide.

Q11. What are amino acids? Explain their different types with one example in each case.
Amino acids are compounds containing both an amino group and a carboxylic acid group, usually on the same (alpha) carbon. By their side chains they are: neutral (glycine), acidic (aspartic acid, glutamic acid), basic (lysine, arginine, histidine), hydroxy (serine), and sulphur-containing (cysteine, methionine). They are also classified as essential (must come from diet, for example lysine) and non-essential (made in the body, for example glycine).

Q12. Write a short note on acidic and basic characters of an amino acid.
An amino acid in solution exists as a zwitterion: the carboxyl group loses a proton and the amino group gains it, so the molecule carries both charges but is neutral overall. In acid solution the amino acid acts as a base and becomes positively charged; in alkaline solution it acts as an acid and becomes negatively charged. At its isoelectric point the amino acid is neutral and has minimum solubility, which is used in separating amino acids.

Q13. What is a peptide bond? Write down the formula of a dipeptide.
A peptide bond is the amide linkage, -CO-NH-, formed between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of another, with loss of water. A dipeptide contains two amino acids joined by one peptide bond, for example glycylglycine: NH2-CH2-CO-NH-CH2-COOH. Longer chains are polypeptides, and very large polypeptides (molecular mass above 10000) are proteins.

Q14. What are zwitter ions?
A zwitterion is a neutral molecule that carries both a positive and a negative charge at different atoms. Amino acids form zwitterions because the acidic -COOH group donates its proton to the basic -NH2 group within the same molecule. Zwitterions explain why amino acids have high melting points and are soluble in water but not in organic solvents.

Q15. What are alpha amino acids, proteins and peptides? How are they related?
Alpha amino acids are the building blocks in which -NH2 and -COOH are attached to the same carbon atom. Two or more amino acids joined by peptide bonds form peptides; a dipeptide has two, a tripeptide three, and a polypeptide many amino acids. Proteins are very large polypeptides, folded into specific shapes, which carry out the structural and catalytic work of the cell.

Q16. Study the facts (a)-(c) and answer: molecular mass of A, identities of A, X and B, five confirming reactions, one large-scale use.
1. Molecular mass of A = 2 x vapour density = 2 x 15 = 30. 2. A is formaldehyde, HCHO; X is methanol, CH3OH; B is formic acid, HCOOH. 3. Confirmations: A gives a silver mirror with Tollen's reagent and restores Schiff's reagent colour; X burns with a blue flame, gives no iodoform test, and with salicylic acid and concentrated H2SO4 gives the wintergreen smell of methyl salicylate. B turns blue litmus red, liberates CO2 with NaHCO3, gives hydrogen with sodium, and reduces Tollen's reagent and Fehling's solution. 4. Large-scale use: formaldehyde is used to make bakelite resins and as a preservative (formalin); methanol is used as a fuel and solvent; formic acid is used in leather tanning and dyeing.

What are macromolecules? Give examples.
Macromolecules are very large molecules made by joining many small units called monomers. Natural examples are proteins, starch, cellulose and nucleic acids. Synthetic examples are nylon, polyester and polythene. They are essential for life and for modern materials.

Why can DNA preserve genetic information from generation to generation?
DNA has a double-stranded helix structure, discovered by Watson and Crick in 1953. The two strands are complementary: adenine pairs with thymine and cytosine with guanine. When a cell divides, each strand acts as a template for a new partner strand. The genetic message is therefore copied exactly into the next generation.

Q4. Explain: (a) addition polymer, (b) condensation polymer, (c) thermoplastic, (d) thermosetting plastic.
An addition polymer is formed by repeated addition of monomer molecules across a double bond, with no by-product; for example, polyethene from ethene. A condensation polymer is formed by monomers joining with loss of a small molecule such as water; for example, nylon 6,6 from adipic acid and hexamethylenediamine. A thermoplastic softens on heating and hardens on cooling, and can be remoulded; a thermosetting plastic becomes permanently hard on heating and cannot be remoulded.

Q5. Write notes on: (a) polyester resins, (b) polyamide resins, (c) epoxy resins.
Polyester resins are condensation polymers of dicarboxylic acids and diols, for example terylene; they are strong, resistant fibres and fabrics. Polyamide resins are condensation polymers of diamines and dicarboxylic acids, for example nylon; they are tough, elastic fibres used in ropes, fabrics and brushes. Epoxy resins are cross-linked polymers formed from epoxides; they are strong adhesives and coatings, resistant to chemicals and heat.

Q6. What is the repeating unit in each of: (a) polystyrene, (b) nylon 6,6, (c) teflon, (d) orlon?
(a) Polystyrene repeating unit: -CH2-CH(C6H5)-, from styrene. (b) Nylon 6,6 repeating unit: -NH-(CH2)6-NH-CO-(CH2)4-CO-, from adipic acid and hexamethylenediamine. (c) Teflon repeating unit: -CF2-CF2-, from tetrafluoroethene. (d) Orlon repeating unit: -CH2-CH(CN)-, from acrylonitrile. The repeating unit is the smallest group of atoms that repeats along the polymer chain.

Q7. What are carbohydrates and how are they classified?
Carbohydrates are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones, or compounds that give them on hydrolysis; they are the most abundant biomolecules on earth. They are classified as monosaccharides (glucose, fructose), oligosaccharides (sucrose, maltose, lactose) and polysaccharides (starch, cellulose, glycogen). Monosaccharides cannot be hydrolysed further, while polysaccharides give many monosaccharide units on hydrolysis.

Q8. Point out one difference between: (a) glucose and fructose, (b) sucrose and maltose, (c) cellulose and starch.
(a) Glucose is an aldohexose (aldehyde group), while fructose is a ketohexose (keto group). (b) Sucrose is a non-reducing sugar (glucose + fructose), while maltose is a reducing sugar (glucose + glucose). (c) Cellulose is a straight-chain polymer of beta-glucose used for structure, while starch is a polymer of alpha-glucose used for storage, with amylose and amylopectin.

Q9. What are lipids? In what way are fats and oils different?
Lipids are naturally occurring organic compounds of plant and animal origin, soluble in organic solvents and insoluble in water. Fats and oils are both glycerides (esters of glycerol with fatty acids); fats are solid at room temperature because they contain mostly saturated fatty acids. Oils are liquid at room temperature because they contain mostly unsaturated fatty acids, with lower melting points.

Q10. Define saponification number and iodine number. Discuss rancidity.
Saponification number is the number of milligrams of KOH needed to saponify one gram of fat or oil; it measures the average molecular mass of the fatty acids. Iodine number is the number of grams of iodine that add to 100 grams of fat or oil; it measures the degree of unsaturation. Rancidity is the unpleasant smell and taste that fats develop when they are oxidised by air or hydrolysed by moisture and enzymes, giving free fatty acids and aldehydes.

Q11. What is the difference between a glycosidic linkage and a peptide linkage?
A glycosidic linkage joins two monosaccharide units through an oxygen atom, as in sucrose, maltose, starch and cellulose. A peptide linkage joins two amino acids through an amide bond, -CO-NH-, as in proteins. The glycosidic linkage is an ether-type (acetal) linkage between sugars, while the peptide linkage is an amide linkage between amino acids.

Q12. What is the chemical nature of enzymes? Discuss the classification of enzymes.
Enzymes are proteins that act as biological catalysts; they are specific, work under mild conditions, and are not used up in the reaction. They are classified by the reaction they catalyse: oxidoreductases (oxidation-reduction), transferases (group transfer), hydrolases (hydrolysis), lyases (addition or removal), isomerases (isomerisation) and ligases (bond formation with ATP). Enzyme activity depends on temperature and pH, with an optimum for each enzyme, and enzymes are inhibited or denatured outside it.

Q13. What are nucleic acids? Write down the role of DNA and RNA in life.
Nucleic acids are polynucleotides made of nucleotide units (sugar + phosphate + nitrogenous base); DNA and RNA are the two types. DNA is the double-stranded store of genetic information; it replicates and passes information from generation to generation. RNA is usually single-stranded and carries out protein synthesis: messenger RNA carries the code, transfer RNA brings amino acids, and ribosomal RNA builds proteins.

Why is the chemical industry important for Pakistan?
Chemical industries convert local raw materials into useful products like fertilizers, cement and soap. Fertilizers raise crop yields and support agriculture, the backbone of the economy. These industries provide jobs and reduce dependence on imports. They also supply medicines, paints and plastics needed in daily life.

Name the main raw materials used by the fertilizer industry in Pakistan.
The main raw material is natural gas, which provides hydrogen for ammonia synthesis. Ammonia is then converted into urea, the chief nitrogenous fertilizer. Rock phosphate is used for phosphatic fertilizers like superphosphate. Sulphur and air are also used in the manufacture of sulphuric and nitric acids.

Q4. What are phosphatic fertilizers? How are they prepared? Mention the role of phosphorus in the growth of plants.
Phosphatic fertilizers supply phosphorus to plants; the main ones are superphosphate and triple phosphate. Superphosphate is prepared by treating phosphate rock with sulphuric acid; triple phosphate by treating phosphate rock with phosphoric acid. Phosphorus stimulates root growth, flowering and fruiting, and is part of ATP and nucleic acids, so it is essential for energy transfer in the plant.

Q5. (a) What are fertilizers? Why are they needed? (b) Discuss the classification of fertilizers and their uses. (c) How is urea manufactured in Pakistan? Describe the process in detail.
Fertilizers are natural or artificial substances containing nutrient elements that improve the growth and productiveness of plants. They are needed because continuous cropping removes nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium from the soil, and the soil alone cannot replace them fast enough. They are classified as nitrogenous (urea, ammonium nitrate), phosphatic (superphosphate, triple phosphate) and potassium fertilizers (potassium chloride, potassium sulphate). Urea is manufactured in Pakistan from liquid ammonia and carbon dioxide: they react to give ammonium carbamate, which dehydrates to urea; the urea solution is concentrated and prilled in a prilling tower.

Q6. (a) What are the prospects of fertilizer industry in Pakistan? (b) What are essential nutrient elements and why are these needed for plant growth? (c) Write down the essential qualities of a good fertilizer.
Pakistan has large reserves of natural gas, limestone and phosphate rock, and a large agricultural sector, so the fertilizer industry has strong prospects for growth. Essential nutrient elements are those without which a plant cannot complete its life cycle: nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium, sulphur, and trace elements such as boron, iron and zinc. They are needed for proteins, chlorophyll, energy transfer, cell walls and enzyme action. A good fertilizer must be water-soluble and readily available to plants, stable in storage, cheap, of suitable concentration, and non-toxic to plants and soil.

Q7. (a) Describe the composition of a good portland cement. (b) Discuss the wet process for the manufacturing of cement. (c) What is setting of cement? Discuss the reactions taking place in the first 24 hours.
Good portland cement contains about 60-67% lime (CaO), 17-25% silica (SiO2), 3-8% alumina (Al2O3), 0.5-6% iron oxide (Fe2O3), with small amounts of magnesia and sulphur trioxide. In the wet process, limestone and clay are ground with water to a slurry, which is fed into a rotary kiln and passes through drying, preheating, decomposition and burning zones to give clinker, which is ground with gypsum to cement. Setting of cement is the hardening of its paste with water into a hard mass. In the first 24 hours, tricalcium aluminate hydrates rapidly and tricalcium silicate hydrates to calcium silicate hydrate gel and calcium hydroxide, giving the first set and early strength.

Q8. What are the essential non-woody raw materials used in the production of pulp and paper in Pakistan?
The essential non-woody raw materials in Pakistan are bagasse (sugarcane residue), rice straw, wheat straw, cotton stalks, and grasses such as kahi and sarkanda. These materials are available in large quantities as agricultural waste and are the main raw materials of the Pakistani paper industry. Their fibres are separated from lignin by pulping, then washed, bleached and formed into paper sheets.

Q9. (a) What are the principal methods of chemical pulping? (b) Describe the neutral sulphite semi-chemical process.
The principal chemical pulping methods are the sulphate (kraft) process, the sulphite process, and the soda process, with the neutral sulphite semi-chemical (NSSC) process for semi-chemical pulp. In the NSSC process, the raw material is cooked with sodium sulphite buffered with sodium carbonate at about 160-180 C in a digester. The cook softens the lignin without fully dissolving it, giving a strong pulp with high yield, which is then washed, refined and bleached.

Q10. (a) What are the common bleaching agents used in paper industry in Pakistan?
Briefly describe the bleaching process. (b) What are the prospects of paper industry in Pakistan? The common bleaching agents in Pakistan are chlorine, sodium hypochlorite, calcium hypochlorite and hydrogen peroxide. In bleaching, the washed pulp is treated in stages with these agents, which oxidise and remove the remaining coloured lignin, giving white pulp. The paper industry in Pakistan has good prospects because demand for paper, packaging and textbooks is growing, but it faces raw-material shortages and needs more recycling of waste paper.

  • The ozone layer protects the earth from harmful ultraviolet rays in the sunlight.

Q6. What is acid rain and how does it affect our environment?
Acid rain is rain containing dissolved oxides of sulphur and nitrogen as acids. These gases come from burning fossil fuels in factories, vehicles and power stations. Acid rain damages crops, forests and buildings made of marble and limestone. It also acidifies lakes and rivers, killing fish and other aquatic life.

Q7. What is smog? Explain the pollutants which are the main cause of photochemical smog.
Smog is a mixture of smoke and fog that hangs over cities and reduces visibility. Photochemical smog forms when nitrogen oxides and hydrocarbons react in sunlight. Ozone, PAN and aldehydes produced in this reaction irritate the eyes and lungs. It also damages plants and rubber goods, and causes breathing difficulties.

Q8. Why is the ozone layer depleting? What will happen when its concentration decreases?
Chlorofluorocarbons released from refrigerators and sprays rise to the stratosphere. Ultraviolet light breaks them down, releasing chlorine atoms that destroy ozone. One chlorine atom can destroy thousands of ozone molecules. Less ozone means more harmful ultraviolet rays reach the earth, causing skin cancer and harming crops.

Q14. How is water purified, i.e., made potable? Discuss in detail.
Raw water is first screened to remove large solids, then left in settling tanks. Alum is added to coagulate fine particles, which settle as sludge. The water is filtered through sand beds to remove remaining suspended matter. Finally it is disinfected with chlorine or ozone to kill germs, making it safe to drink.

lessons.notes_html:
Q4. Discuss in detail the components of the environment.
The environment consists of four components: the atmosphere (gases around the earth), the hydrosphere (all water), the lithosphere (rocks and soil), and the biosphere (all living things). These components interact: air, water, soil and life exchange matter and energy continuously. Environmental chemistry studies the sources, reactions, transport and effects of pollutants in these components.

Q5. Describe the natural and human sources of carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides and sulphur oxides.
Carbon monoxide comes naturally from volcanoes and forest fires, and from human sources such as automobile exhaust, incomplete combustion of fuels and industrial furnaces. Nitrogen oxides come naturally from lightning and bacterial action, and from vehicles, power stations and furnaces burning fuel at high temperature. Sulphur oxides come naturally from volcanoes and decaying organic matter, and from burning coal and oil containing sulphur, smelters and refineries.

Q9. How is oil spillage affecting the marine life?
Oil spilled on the sea forms a layer on the surface that blocks light and oxygen from reaching marine plants and animals. Birds and mammals coated with oil lose insulation and buoyancy, and many die from poisoning when they clean themselves. Oil also damages beaches, fishing grounds and coral reefs, and its toxic components poison fish and shellfish for years.

Q10. How are detergents a threat to aquatic animal life?
Detergents contain phosphates and surfactants that wash into rivers and lakes. Phosphates cause algal blooms, which use up dissolved oxygen when they decay, suffocating fish and other aquatic animals. Surfactants damage the gills and cell membranes of aquatic animals, and detergents mobilise bound toxic metals from sediments into the water.

Q12. Explain how pesticides are dangerous to human beings.
Pesticides are toxic chemicals that kill pests, but they also poison farm workers, contaminate food and drinking water, and accumulate in the food chain. They can damage the nervous system, liver and kidneys, cause cancer and birth defects, and kill useful insects, birds and fish. Persistent pesticides such as DDT remain in soil and water for years and build up in the fatty tissues of animals and humans.

Q13. Discuss industrial waste effluents.
Industrial waste effluents are liquid wastes discharged by factories, containing acids, alkalis, heavy metals, oils, dyes and toxic organic chemicals. When discharged untreated into rivers, they kill aquatic life, make water unfit for drinking and irrigation, and contaminate soil and groundwater. They must be treated before discharge: neutralised, settled, filtered and biologically treated, and heavy metals must be removed.

Q15. What are leachates?
Leachates are liquids formed when water percolates through solid waste in a landfill, dissolving and suspending contaminants. They contain dissolved organic matter, ammonia, hydrogen sulphide, heavy metals and disease-causing microorganisms. If a landfill is not properly lined, leachate leaks into soil and groundwater and contaminates drinking water supplies.

Q16. Explain the process of incineration of industrial waste.
Industrial and hazardous waste is incinerated at high temperature in a rotary kiln, which accepts liquid, solid or sludge waste. The waste burns in a rotating chamber, and the gases pass to a non-rotating (secondary) chamber kept at 950-1300 C, where combustion is completed. The heat may be used to raise steam, and the remaining ash is disposed of in a landfill; incineration is not clean, because it produces air pollution, toxic ash and dioxins.
